# AirSQL Help (all pages)

> AirSQL is a free, open-source Mac app (macOS 13.1 or later, Apple silicon and Intel) for MySQL and MariaDB: connections direct or through SSH tunnels, jump hosts and proxies, a SQL console, a data grid with safe editing, schema tools, client tools (mysql, mysqldump), compare and reconcile, and access for AI agents over MCP at the level the person at the Mac sets for each connection. Nothing is written to a server without the person's Run, Apply or approval, and agents never see saved passwords.

- Install: `brew install --cask kleash/tap/airsql` (or the zip from https://github.com/kleash/airsql/releases).

Every page of AirSQL Help (https://kleash.github.io/airsql/), then the agent guide.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/

# AirSQL Help

AirSQL is a Mac app for MySQL and MariaDB.

![The AirSQL window: saved connections and a shop database's tables on the left, its newest orders in the grid](assets/screenshots/main-light.png)

More pictures: the [README](https://github.com/kleash/airsql#screenshots).

- [Install AirSQL](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/install.html): with Homebrew or from the download.
- [Getting started](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/getting-started.html): add a connection, find your way around the window.
- [Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html): the look, the editor and grid, connections, safety checks, agents, client tools and
  Liquibase.
- [Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html): the sheet that shows every change first.
- [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html): servers whose certificate macOS doesn't know.
- [The SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html): every statement AirSQL sends, with passwords masked.
- [Read-only queries](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html): what an agent's query, or a read-only connection, may run, and why one is
  refused.
- [The SQL console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html): write and run SQL, results, transactions, history and the SQL log.
- [Connections and routes](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html): add and edit connections, SSH tunnels, jump hosts, proxies and folders.
- [Browse a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/navigator.html): the tree, the database view, table commands, find text and the process list.
- [A table's rows](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html): load, filter, search, sort, edit, apply, copy and export a table's rows.
- [Read the data in a grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html): the status bar's figures, the value panel, Record View, Transpose, Display
  As, heatmaps, View As, charts and Column Summary, in a table's rows and a query's results.
- [Change tables, views and routines](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html): the table editor, views and routines as CREATE code, and the ER
  diagram.
- [Export, restore, copy and import](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html): your mysqldump and mysql, or AirSQL's own export and runner; copy
  to another server; CSV import.
- [Compare two databases](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html): structure and data, side by side, and a sync script you review first; or two
  results, or a result with a table, row by row.
- [AI agents](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html): let Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Claude Desktop read your schemas and run read-only queries, at
  the access you choose.
- [Liquibase changelogs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html): a database as formatted SQL changesets, and any change saved as one.
- [Keyboard shortcuts](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/shortcuts.html): every command's shortcut.
- [Accessibility](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/accessibility.html): VoiceOver, the keyboard, motion and text size.
- [Privacy and security](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/privacy-security.html): what AirSQL connects to, where passwords are kept, what agents may do.
- [Troubleshooting](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/troubleshooting.html): when a connection fails, and how to report a problem.

Every button and menu command says what it does when you hold the pointer over it.

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/install.html

# Install AirSQL

AirSQL needs macOS 13.1 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. It is free, and it needs no account.

## With Homebrew

```sh
brew install --cask kleash/tap/airsql
```

Later, `brew upgrade --cask airsql` updates it.

## From the download

1. Download **AirSQL-X.Y.Z.zip** from the [latest release](https://github.com/kleash/airsql/releases/latest).
2. Open the zip, then drag **AirSQL** to your **Applications** folder.
3. Open AirSQL. Apple has checked it (it is notarized), so it opens like any app.

To check the download first, see [Check a download](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/privacy-security.html#check-a-download).

## Remove AirSQL

Drag AirSQL from Applications to the Bin (with Homebrew: `brew uninstall --cask airsql`). Your connections and settings
stay in `~/Library/Application Support/AirSQL`, and saved passwords in your Keychain (the item named
`com.kleash.airsql` in Keychain Access), until you delete them. `brew uninstall --zap --cask airsql` deletes the
settings too.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/getting-started.html

# Getting started

## Add your first connection

Choose **File ▸ New Connection…** (⌘N), or **Add Connection…** on the first screen: the connection appears in the
sidebar, and its summary shows where it goes and how it logs in.

Passwords stay in your Keychain. A connection coloured **Production** starts with stricter safety checks
([Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html#safety)).

## No server yet?

To try AirSQL with nothing installed but [Docker](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/), start a throwaway
MariaDB on this Mac:

```sh
docker run --name try-mariadb -e MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=try-it -p 127.0.0.1:3306:3306 -d mariadb:11
```

Add a connection to host `127.0.0.1`, user `root`, password `try-it`, then open
[demo-shop.sql](https://github.com/kleash/airsql/blob/main/scripts/demo-shop.sql) with **File ▸ Open…** and press **Run
All** (⇧⌘↩): it fills a small shop to look around in. `docker rm -f try-mariadb` removes it all.

## Run a query

Double-click the connection to connect, then choose **File ▸ New Query** (⌘T). Pick a database in the toolbar, type a
statement, and press ⌘↩: the results show under the editor. See [Query tabs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html).

## Edit rows

Click a table in the sidebar to see its rows, and double-click a cell to change it. Your edits wait, marked in the grid,
until you press **Apply** (⌘S), which shows the SQL first; **Revert** takes them back. See [Table data](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html).

## The window

- **The sidebar** lists your connections. Click one to see its summary, double-click it to connect, right-click it for
  everything else (Duplicate, Colour, Delete…). Hold ⌘ or ⇧ to select several.
- **The tabs** hold your queries and tables. When more are open than fit, the arrow at the end of the strip lists them all. Double-click a tab to rename it; middle-click it to close it; right-click it
  to close the others or all of them, or to duplicate it. ⌘W closes the tab shown, or the window when it has no tab, as
  it does in Settings, the SQL log and Compare. ⇧⌘T brings back the tab you closed last. ⌘P (**Quick Open…**) goes to a
  table, view or connection by part of its name.
- **The toolbar** (right-click it for **Icon and Text**, or **View ▸ Customize Toolbar…**) shows the connection and database a tab works on (choose another in either pop-up), Run (⌘↩), Run
  All (⇧⌘↩), Explain, the transaction mode and isolation level, Commit, Roll Back and Cancel. A button that can't act
  now is dimmed, and its tooltip says why.
- **The status bar** shows the route to the server, its version, an open transaction, the work running now (click it to
  cancel), what agents are doing, and the SQL log. Click an item for details; right-click it to copy it. When the
  window is narrow, the server's version, the route and then the agents' item make room first; an open transaction's
  warning keeps all its text, and a grid's row count stays.

## Tips

- Nothing is written to a database until you press Run or Apply.
- ⌘1 to ⌘9 show your tabs; ⇧⌘[ and ⇧⌘] step through them.
- **Help ▸ Report a Problem** opens a form with your versions filled in.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html

# Settings

Open **AirSQL ▸ Settings…** (⌘,). Changes are saved as you make them.

## General

- **Appearance**: **System** follows the Mac's light or dark mode; **Light** always uses Porcelain, **Dark** Deep
  Water.
- **Settings folder**: where your connections and settings are kept. Passwords are in your Keychain, never there.

## Editor

- **Wrap long lines**: wrap them at the editor's edge instead of scrolling sideways; on at first (**View ▸ Word Wrap** too).

- **Text size**: the SQL editor's (13 pt at first). **View ▸ Bigger** (⌘+) and **Smaller** (⌘−) change it for a
  moment; **Actual Size** (⌘0) goes back to this size.

## Grid

- **Text size**: the grid's (12 pt at first), open grids' too. ⌘+, ⌘− and ⌘0 change it the same way for the grid with
  the focus; a grid made bigger or smaller keeps its size until ⌘0.
- **Rows per page**: how many rows a table or result loads at a time (1,000 by default).
- **Load All asks above**: Load All asks first when a table has more rows than this (100,000 by default), since every
  row is then held in memory.
- **NULL shown as**: how empty values look in the grid, open grids' too.
- **Transpose results with one row**: a query result with a single row opens turned on its side, one line per
  column (on by default).

## Connections

- **Load details up to … tables**: on a server with more tables than this, a database's columns, indexes and keys load
  when you open it, so connecting stays quick.

## Safety

What asks first before data changes. These are the defaults; a connection can have its own (every switch and limit
below, in its Safety tab), and a connection coloured Production starts with a strict preset.

| Setting | Default | Production |
|---|---|---|
| Ask before UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE | on | on |
| Ask before any write from the query tab | off | on |
| Show the SQL before the grid's Apply | off | on |
| Ask before DROP or TRUNCATE (a database's name is always typed) | on | on, table names typed too |
| Ask before restoring into a database that has tables | on | on |
| Leave DROP and DELETE out of sync scripts unless ticked | always | always |
| Ask before agents change anything | on | on |
| Agents' rows per query and time limit | 10,000 and 30 s | 1,000 and 15 s |
| Warn when a transaction stays open | 15 minutes | 5 minutes |
| Ask before sorting a large table by a column without an index | on | on |
| Warn when closing with an open transaction or pending edits | on | on |

**Restore Defaults** puts every switch back. Read-only is a switch of each connection. Agents can read these settings
but never change them.

## Agents

- **Allow AI agents to use AirSQL**: off until you turn it on. Agents never see passwords.
- **Connections**: what agents may do with each connection: Off (where every connection starts), Schema, Schema + read,
  or Schema + read + analytics; and **Sample rows**, which lets them see a few rows of each table. Right-click a
  connection for the same choices; double-click it to open its settings at the Agents tab.
- **Exports**: the only folder agents save files in.
- **Add to Claude Code…** and **Add to Gemini CLI…**: show the change to that program's settings that adds AirSQL, and
  make it when you click Add. **Copy** gives the command other MCP clients start.

More in [AI agents](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html).

## Client Tools

The `mysql` (or `mariadb`) and `mysqldump` (or `mariadb-dump`) programs AirSQL runs. Leave them empty to let AirSQL
find them: it looks in Homebrew's folders, `/usr/local/mysql/bin`, MAMP and your `PATH`, and picks for each server the
tools of its family and version. Under each field the pane says which program and version it found, or why there is
none or it can't be used; **Found** lists every tool on this Mac, and **Find Again** looks again after you install or
update some. See [Export, restore, copy and import](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html).

## Liquibase

Who changesets are by, how their ids are made, whether a changelog is one file or a folder, how procedures, functions,
triggers and events are kept whole, DEFINER, and `--rollback`. See [Liquibase changelogs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html#settings).


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html

# Check SQL before it runs

Some changes show their SQL in a sheet before anything runs: applying edits in a table, changing a table's structure,
dropping or renaming, restoring a dump, and sync scripts.

- **Warnings** say what else will happen, such as rows deleted in other tables (ON DELETE CASCADE), or a table whose
  engine can't roll back.
- A change on a **Production** connection says so in red.
- To drop a database (and, on Production, a table), type its name first.
- When an **agent** asked for the change, the sheet names it. Nothing runs until you approve it; **Decline** refuses it.
- **Save as Liquibase changeset** (a table's edited rows, the table and object editors, dropping, emptying or renaming
  in the sidebar, and sync scripts) saves the statements as a changeset in a changelog once they have run (see
  [Liquibase changelogs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html)). In the query tab, use **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…**.
- **Copy SQL** copies the statements. **Cancel** changes nothing.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html

# Trust a server

When a server's certificate isn't one macOS trusts (it is self-signed, or from your company's own certificate
authority), AirSQL shows its SHA-256 fingerprint and asks before connecting.

1. Compare the fingerprint with the one the server's administrator gave you.
2. If they match, choose **Trust**. AirSQL remembers the certificate for this connection (the editor's TLS tab shows
   it, with **Forget**) and refuses any other.
3. If they don't, choose **Cancel**: you may not be talking to the server you think.

If a trusted server later shows another certificate, AirSQL says so and doesn't connect unless you choose **Trust the
New Certificate**. Do that only when the administrator told you the certificate changed.

## SSH hosts

The first time a connection goes through an SSH host, AirSQL shows the host's key fingerprint the same way. **Trust**
lets ssh remember the key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If the key ever changes, ssh refuses to connect and AirSQL says
which host it was: ask its administrator before removing the old key from `known_hosts`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html

# The SQL log

AirSQL writes every statement it sends to a server into one file on your Mac, just before the statement goes out.
Use it to see exactly what AirSQL did: what a query tab ran, what a table edit applied, what the navigator asked the
server for.

## Where it is

`~/Library/Logs/AirSQL/SQL.log`. Only you can read it (file mode 0600). At 10 MB it becomes `SQL.1.log`, replacing the
one before, and a new file starts. It stays on your Mac: AirSQL sends it nowhere.

## What a line says

```
2026-11-03 14:03:12.345 [Shop production main:12] SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 7
```

- the time;
- the connection's name;
- the session: **main** (query tabs), **data** (table tabs and their edits), **schema** (the navigator), **agent**
  (AI agents), **tools** (client tools and compare), **cancel** (the short connection that stops a running statement);
- the statement's number in that session. The server sees the same number in a comment at the start of the statement,
  `/* airsql:main:12 */`, so you can find it in the server's process list.

Lines that start with `--` are AirSQL's own notes: connected (server version, thread, TLS), disconnected, connection
lost, reconnected (and whether an open transaction was rolled back), the number of a statement's error, and
"startup SQL (2 statements)".

## What is never in it

- **Passwords you log in with**: they go to the server only during the login, never as SQL.
- **Passwords and keys inside statements**: replaced with `<secret>`, as MySQL hides them in its own logs: the value
  after `IDENTIFIED BY`, `SET PASSWORD … =`, `MASTER_PASSWORD` or `SOURCE_PASSWORD`, `PASSWORD '…'` in `CREATE SERVER`,
  everything inside `PASSWORD(…)`, and the key of `AES_ENCRYPT`, `AES_DECRYPT`, `DES_ENCRYPT`, `DES_DECRYPT`, `ENCODE`,
  `DECODE` and `ENCRYPT`. A value set for a column named like `password` is hidden too.
- **A connection's startup SQL**: only how many statements it had, since it may hold secrets.
- **Error messages**: only their numbers, because a syntax error quotes the statement it failed on.
- **Results**: rows never go into the log.

Very long statements (an import's big `INSERT`) are cut after 60,000 bytes.

⌘F opens a find bar over the log while its text has the focus.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html

# Read-only queries

Where only reading is allowed, such as a query from an AI agent or anything run on a
[read-only connection](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html#add-or-edit-a-connection), AirSQL first checks that the statement can only read.
The check is strict on purpose: when in doubt it refuses, and it says why in one line.

## What passes

One statement at a time (a `;` at the end is fine):

- `SELECT`, with `UNION`, subqueries and `WITH … SELECT`;
- `SHOW …`;
- `DESCRIBE`, `DESC` or `EXPLAIN` of a table; `EXPLAIN` of a `SELECT` (`FORMAT=JSON` and `FORMAT=TREE` too);
  `EXPLAIN FOR CONNECTION` and a connection number.

## What is refused, wherever it appears

- More than one statement, and every other kind of statement: `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `SET`, `CALL`, `DO`, `CREATE` and
  the rest, and `WITH …` followed by anything but `SELECT`.
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which runs the statement, and `EXPLAIN` of `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `REPLACE`.
- `INTO` (a file or variables), `FOR UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE` and `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`.
- Optimizer hints, `/*+ … */`: they can lift the server's time limit (`MAX_EXECUTION_TIME`).
- Temporary tables: they can be written even in a read-only transaction.
- Setting a variable with `:=`, and moving a sequence on (`NEXT VALUE FOR`, `NEXTVAL`, `SETVAL`).
- Any function other than the built-in ones that only compute. So `SLEEP`, `BENCHMARK`, `GET_LOCK` and the other
  locks, `LOAD_FILE`, `LAST_INSERT_ID` and the waits for replication are refused, and so are user-defined functions,
  stored functions (`shop.bonus(…)`, or any name AirSQL doesn't know) and function names in quotes.

The text inside executable comments, `/*! … */` and `/*M! … */`, counts as code, whatever server version it names.

## Backslashes and double quotes

The check reads a backslash in a string as the server does: as an escape, unless the session's sql_mode has
`NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES`. Double-quoted text with a backslash in it is refused either way: with `ANSI_QUOTES` it is a
name, where a backslash escapes nothing, so the server could end it somewhere else. Write strings in single quotes.

## A safeguard, not the only one

For a hard guarantee, connect agents with a database user that can only read.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html

# The SQL console

A query tab (the SQL console) is where you write and run SQL on one connection. Its statements run one at a time, on a
session of its own, so a long query in one tab leaves the others free.

## Open a query tab

- **File ▸ New Query** (⌘T), the **+** at the end of the tabs, or **New Query** on a connection's menu opens an empty query tab on the selected connection. **New Query** on a database's menu (or ⌘T while a database is selected in the
  sidebar) makes that database the current one first.
- **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) opens .sql files, each in a query tab of its own. You can also drop .sql files anywhere on the
  window or on AirSQL's Dock icon, or open them with AirSQL from Finder: they open on the connection shown.
- **File ▸ Save** (⌘S) saves the tab's text to its file; **Save As…** to a new one. A tab with unsaved text shows a
  dot instead of its close button.
- Drag a result's tab to put the results in another order.
- Drag a tab along the strip to move it. Past ⌘9, the **Window** menu lists every tab.
- Double-click a query tab's tab (or press F2 while its editor has the focus) to give it a name of your own.
- When you quit, the open query tabs are kept, unsaved text included, and come back the next time you open AirSQL. The
  other tabs come back too: see [Getting back to your tabs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/navigator.html#getting-back-to-your-tabs).
- **File ▸ Open Recent** lists the .sql files you had open lately. A file opens on the connection you last used it with.
- A file that isn't UTF-8 opens by its byte-order mark, else as Windows Latin 1, and Messages says so; Save writes UTF-8.
- If a file changes on disk, its tab follows, and ⌘Z brings back what it showed; with unsaved edits, Messages warns instead.
- **Query ▸ Change Connection…** runs the tab's statements on another connection. A tab with no connection, such as a
  file opened with nothing selected, takes the one the toolbar shows.

## Write SQL

- Keywords, names, strings, numbers and comments have their own colours; the brackets around the cursor are marked.
- A quote, comment or bracket left open is underlined in red a moment after you stop typing, and hovering over it says
  what's missing. No server is asked.
- A table or column that isn't in the schema AirSQL has read is underlined in red the same way, and hovering over it
  says what wasn't found. It's only advice: **Run** still runs, and nothing is sent to the server to check. When
  AirSQL isn't sure it says nothing: a database whose details aren't loaded yet, temporary tables and tables made or
  altered in the same text or session, CTEs, derived tables, and any statement other than a plain SELECT, INSERT,
  REPLACE, UPDATE or DELETE. Columns are checked only when every table in the statement is known. If a table is new,
  **Refresh** the schema and the underline goes.
- **Completion** opens as you type: after FROM or JOIN the tables and views, after JOIN first the joins that foreign
  keys give (`orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`), after `alias.` that table's columns, after USE the databases, and
  elsewhere the statement's columns, functions and keywords. ↑ and ↓ choose, Return or Tab inserts, Escape closes;
  ⌥⎋ opens it anywhere. It comes from what AirSQL already read of the schema: nothing is sent to the server while you
  type.
- **View ▸ Query Helpers** shows beside the editor the columns of the tables the statement at the cursor names, the
  server's functions by kind, and the keywords. Double-click one to put it in at the cursor, or drag it into the editor
  (a column's name comes quoted where it needs to be, as completion puts it in).
- **Edit ▸ Find** (⌘F) and **Find and Replace** (⌥⌘F) find in the editor, with **Regular Expression** and **Match
  Case**. With a regular expression, `$1`, `$2`… in the replacement put in its groups. **Replace All** is one change
  that **Undo** takes back.
- Typing `(`, `[` or a quote adds its partner, or wraps the selection; typing the partner steps over it, and Delete
  between an empty pair takes both.
- **Edit ▸ Go to Line…** (⌃G) goes to the line a message names. Long lines wrap at the editor's edge; **View ▸ Word Wrap**
  (also in Settings ▸ Editor) turns that off, for sideways scrolling.
- **Edit ▸ Comment Lines** (⌘/) comments the selected lines out with `--`, or takes the comment away. **Shift Right**
  (⌘]) and **Shift Left** (⌘[) indent; so do Tab and ⇧Tab on several lines.
- **Query ▸ Format SQL** (⌥⇧⌘F) puts each main clause on a line of its own and reserved words in capitals. It changes
  nothing else: names, values, comments and `/*! … */` code stay exactly as they are, and statements inside a
  `DELIMITER` block are left alone. If it couldn't do that, it leaves the SQL as it was and says so.
- **View ▸ Bigger** (⌘+), **Smaller** (⌘−) and **Actual Size** change the text size for a moment; Settings ▸ Editor
  sets it for good.

## Run it

| To run | Press |
|---|---|
| The statement at the cursor, or the selected text | ⌘↩ (or ⌃F9) |
| Only the selected text | Query ▸ Run Selection |
| The selected text as it stands, not split on `;` | Query ▸ Run Selection as One Statement |
| The smallest query in brackets around the cursor | Query ▸ Run Subquery |
| The statement at the cursor and every one after it | Query ▸ Run from Cursor |
| Every statement | ⇧⌘↩ (or F9) |
| Stop the statement that is running | ⌘. (Query ▸ Cancel) |

The statement that ran is highlighted for a moment, so there is no "which statement?" question. Statements are split
on `;`, or on the delimiter a `DELIMITER` line sets, and sent one after another. If one fails with others to come, a
sheet asks whether to **Stop**, **Skip** it, or **Skip All** that fail from there on. Each
statement that ran then shows a tick, or a cross if it failed, and its time at the end of its line, until you change it
or run again.

While a statement runs, the bar above the results shows which one and for how long, with **Cancel**; the status bar
lists it too. Cancel stops only that statement: AirSQL checks the server is still running it before it stops it. A
connection can have a query timeout: a statement that runs longer is stopped the same way, and Messages says so.
The time shown covers the whole run: waiting its turn, the server's work and fetching every row. After an `UPDATE`,
Messages counts the rows changed; the server's note beside it says how many matched.

If you've gone to another app and a run of 10 seconds or more ends, AirSQL's Dock icon bounces once and a notification
says which tab finished. It never shows the SQL. Turn the notification off in System Settings ▸ Notifications.

### Parameters

A statement with `?` or `:name` in its code, not in a string or comment, asks for their values before it runs. The same
`:name` takes one value. A number or `NULL` goes in as it is; anything else goes in as quoted text, so a value can't
become code. The tab remembers the values for the next run. AirSQL fills them in before sending, so Messages, the SQL
log and the history show the final SQL, and the read-only and safety checks see it too.

### Sessions

Each query tab opens its own session the first time it runs something, and closes it when the tab closes. So each tab
has its own transaction and current database, and several tabs can run at once; Cancel stops only the tab's own
statement. A temporary table belongs to one session, so another tab can't see it.

To see temporary tables across tabs, turn on **Query tabs share one session** on the connection's Options tab. The
connection's query tabs then use one session, with one transaction and one database, and while one runs a statement the
others wait.

If the server is within five connections of its `max_connections`, or refuses another, a tab shares the connection's
main session instead of opening its own, and Messages says so.

If a tab's session is lost, the next Run says so, and says if an open transaction was rolled back, and runs nothing.
Run again to open a new session.

### The current database

Statements run in the tab's current database, which the toolbar's database pop-up shows and the sidebar shows in bold
while the tab is on show. Choose another in the pop-up, double-click one in the sidebar, or type `USE`: all three change
it for the tab on show, and the other tabs keep theirs. A new tab starts in the database shown. A database chosen in the
pop-up or the sidebar is made current with `USE` just before the next statement runs (Messages shows it), so a run under
way is never switched midway; if that `USE` fails, nothing runs. On a connection whose tabs share one session, they
share the current database too.

## Results and Messages

- Each result set gets a **result tab** under the editor, named after the comment just above its query (`-- Top
  customers` names it "Top customers"), else "Result 1", with its rows and columns. The next run replaces the result
  tabs, unless you **pin** one (right-click it, or Query ▸ Pin Result); a result with edits not yet applied stays too.
  A tab's ✕ closes it. **Query ▸ Show Next Result** (⌥⌘]) and **Show Previous Result** (⌥⌘[) move along the tabs,
  Messages included.
- **Query ▸ Run Result Again** (⇧⌘R) runs the shown result's statement once more and puts the new rows in its tab,
  which keeps its name and pin. **Copy Result's Query** copies the statement. **View ▸ Refresh Every** does it every few
  seconds, for a statement that only reads, until it fails or you choose Off.
- **Query ▸ Keep Results of Each Run** leaves the tab's earlier results in place at each run.
- Double-click a result tab to rename it; right-click it to run it again, pin, rename or close it, export its rows, or compare it
  with another result or a table (**Compare With…**, see [Compare](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html#compare-two-results-or-a-result-with-a-table)).
  When more tabs are open than fit, scroll the tabs sideways.
- **Messages** lists when and what each statement did: its rows or the rows it changed, how long it took, the server's
  warnings, or its error and the line it points to (that line is marked red beside the editor, the place the server
  names is underlined in red, and hovering over it shows the message, until you change the text). Double-click a message
  to select its statement.
- A result keeps at most its first 100,000 rows; the tab then says it is cut short.
- **Edit ▸ Find** (⌘F) with a result's rows focused finds values in them, as in a [table tab](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html): ⌘G and ⇧⌘G
  move between matches, and Options has Match Case, Regular Expression, Whole Words and Filter Rows. Replace is for
  table tabs.
- **Filter, search and sort a result** on its rows, at once, without running the query again: right-click a cell for
  **Quick Filter** (the same conditions as in a [table tab](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html#filter-search-and-sort), Type a Value…
  included), a header for **Filter by Values…** (the values in the rows shown, with their counts) or **Add to Sort**
  and **Sort by Columns…** (⇧-click a header's arrow adds to the sort too), or click a value in **Column Summary…**. **Data ▸ Search All Columns** (⇧⌘E) keeps the rows with the text
  in any column and tints it. A bar over the rows shows while a filter or a search is on: **Local · 12 of 200 rows**,
  the conditions as SQL, and the search; its ⓧ or **Data ▸ Clear Filter** shows every row again. Copy and Export Rows…
  take the rows shown. The **?** at the right of the result tabs opens [Read the data in a grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html).

### Edit a result

The rows of a `SELECT` from one table can be edited when the result includes the table's key (its primary key, or a
unique key whose columns can't be NULL); so can an inner join's when every table's key is in it. The status bar says
**Editable** or **Read-only**, with the reason in its tooltip; double-click a read-only cell to see why (an outer join,
`GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `UNION`, a subquery in `FROM`, a self-join, a column worked out by the query, or a row of the
"one" side of a join that shows in several result rows).

- Double-click a cell (or start typing) to change it. As in a table tab, a boolean toggles, ENUM and SET pick from their
  members, ↑ and ↓ step a date, and a foreign key has its drop-down. **Cut** (⌘X), **Paste** (⌘V), **Set NULL** (⌥⌘N),
  **Set DEFAULT**, **Insert Value** and, in a one-table result, **Delete Rows** (⌘⌫) work too. Paste fills the rows the
  result has, and pastes nothing if a value doesn't fit its column. Values are checked by their column's type as you type. Changes wait, marked in colour,
  with a bar over the rows counting them; **Undo**, **Redo**, **Revert** and **Revert All** take them back.
- **Apply** (⌘S while the rows have the keyboard, or the bar's button) writes them in one transaction on the
  connection's data session, each statement checked to change exactly its row. A join's changes always show the SQL
  first; so do changes on connections whose **Settings ▸ Safety** asks for the preview, and deletes that cascade. If the query tab has a transaction open, Apply asks you to commit or roll it back first, so it doesn't wait for its locks.
- After Apply, the edited rows are read back from the server, so the result shows what was stored; deleted rows go.
  New rows and pasting are for a table tab: open the table to add rows.
- Edits not applied are never discarded unasked: the next run keeps their result tab, and disconnecting asks first;
  so do closing the result, closing the query tab and quitting, unless the connection's Safety settings don't warn on
  close.
- On a read-only connection nothing can be edited.

### Edit INSERT statements as a table

Select one or more `INSERT … VALUES` statements of one table (or put the cursor in one) and choose **Query ▸ Edit as
Table** (also in the editor's right-click menu). The table opens in its tab with each row as a new row, a pending
change: strings and numbers as their values, `NULL`, `DEFAULT`, and anything else (such as `NOW()`) as SQL the server
works out. Change them as you like, then **Apply**: it always shows the SQL first. Nothing runs from the query tab.

## Transactions

- **Auto-commit** (the toolbar's transaction pop-up, or Query ▸ Transaction Mode) commits each statement by itself. In
  **Manual**, your changes wait in a transaction until you press **Commit**, or **Roll Back** to undo them. Leaving
  Manual with changes waiting asks first whether to commit them or roll them back.
- The **isolation level** (in the transaction pop-up, or Query ▸ Isolation Level) sets how the tab's transactions see
  others' changes: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read or Serializable, set on the tab's session with
  `SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL`. Until you choose one, the server's own applies (usually Repeatable Read).
- The toolbar's Run, Commit, Roll Back and Cancel are on only when the query tab can do them now; when one is off, its
  tooltip says why (not connected, no transaction open, nothing running).
- While a transaction is open, the status bar says so, with the number of rows changed, and how long it has been open
  once that passes the time set in Settings ▸ Safety.
- Closing a query tab with a transaction open asks first: **Commit**, **Roll Back** or keep the tab. On a connection
  whose tabs share one session, only its last tab asks.
- New sessions start in Auto-commit at the server's isolation level, unless the connection's Options tab says **Start
  query tabs in Manual Commit** or chooses an **Isolation level**.
- Quitting AirSQL with a transaction open asks first too, in one sheet with any table changes and result edits not yet
  applied.

On a [read-only connection](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html#add-or-edit-a-connection), Run, Explain and Profile refuse any statement
AirSQL can't prove only reads (SELECT, WITH … SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN and USE pass), and Messages says why.

## What asks first

The safety settings (Settings ▸ Safety, or a connection's own) decide which statements ask before they run. The SQL
shows in a sheet, with what it will do:

- an UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE, which changes every row of its table;
- DROP and TRUNCATE; dropping a database needs its name typed, and so does dropping or emptying a table where the
  connection says so (the Production preset does);
- on a connection where every write asks (the Production preset), any statement that may change data.

## History, the SQL log, plans and profiles

- **Query ▸ Query History** (⌘Y) lists the statements run on the tab's connection, newest first. Type to search;
  Return or a double-click puts one in the editor at the cursor, and a click shows it whole below the list. Click a
  header to sort, ⌘-click to select several; a right-click also opens them in a new tab or deletes them from the
  history. Passwords in statements are masked before they are kept, as in the SQL log. **All connections** searches
  every connection's statements, with a column saying which.
- **File ▸ Local History…** lists the states a .sql file was saved in (the last 50, kept on this Mac only). Click one to read
  it; **Restore** puts it in the editor, ⌘Z takes it back, and nothing is written until you save.
- **Query ▸ Sessions…** lists every session AirSQL has open on the connection: what uses it, its thread on the server, its
  database, and whether it is running or holds a transaction.
- **View ▸ SQL Log** (⌥⌘L) shows every statement AirSQL sent, as they come. See [the SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html).
- **Query ▸ Explain** (⌥⌘E) shows how the server would run the statement at the cursor, without running it. **Operations**
  lists the steps as a tree with the server's rows and cost; click a header to sort the steps of each level, and the
  steps that take a large share are marked in orange. **Table** is the server's EXPLAIN, **Tree** the steps as text and
  **Raw** the server's own answer, to copy.
- **Query ▸ Explain Analyze** (⌥⇧⌘E) runs the statement and adds what really happened: rows read, time and loops. It uses
  `ANALYZE FORMAT=JSON` on MariaDB and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on MySQL 8.0.18 or later. As it really runs the statement, a
  read-only connection refuses it, and a statement that may write always asks first.
- **Query ▸ Profile** runs the statement and shows where the server spent its time. On MySQL 8 and later it reads
  performance_schema: the statement's stages where the server records them, else its own figures (time, lock time,
  rows examined and sent, temporary tables, sorts and full scans). Elsewhere it shows SHOW PROFILE's steps, as it does
  on MySQL 8 when performance_schema is off or your login can't read it, with a note saying so.
- **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…** saves the selected statements (or the one at the cursor) as a Liquibase changeset in a
  changelog you choose. See [Liquibase changelogs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html).


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html

# Connections and routes

A connection is a MySQL or MariaDB server AirSQL remembers: its address, the login, how to reach it (its route) and
a few options. Passwords go in your Keychain, never in AirSQL's files.

## Add or edit a connection

Choose **File ▸ New Connection…** (⌘N), or select a connection and choose **Connection ▸ Edit…**. The editor has six
tabs:

- **General**: a name, the sidebar folder, a colour (Production also turns on the strict safety checks), the host and
  port, or for a server on this Mac its socket file, the user and password, the database to open, and a comment (what
  it is for, who to ask). Tick **Ask at each connect** to type the user and password each time; they are kept until
  you disconnect and never saved.
- **TLS**: how the connection is encrypted. A new connection to `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` starts with TLS off, as such
  servers rarely offer it and nothing leaves this Mac; any other host, or any route, starts with the strict check. **Encrypt, check certificate and host name** is the safe choice: the server must
  show a certificate for the host name you typed, even through a tunnel. A server whose certificate macOS doesn't know
  shows its fingerprint when you connect (see [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html)). Add a CA certificate for a
  private certificate authority, and a client certificate and key for a server that asks for one. **PAM or LDAP
  login** allows the plain-text login such accounts need, only over TLS that proves the server.
- **SSH and Proxy**: the route (below).
- **Options**: read-only (below), the compressed protocol, a query timeout, how query tabs use sessions and start their transactions (see [Sessions](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html#sessions)), the databases shown (names or patterns
  such as `shop, reports_*`), startup SQL that runs after each login (for example `SET time_zone = '+00:00';`), and the
  connection's own client tools (empty: Settings ▸ Client Tools' choice; each says which program and version it is, or
  why it can't be used).
- **Safety**: safety checks of the connection's own: every switch and limit of [Settings ▸ Safety](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html#safety),
  starting from the ones that applied, with a slider mark beside its name in the sidebar.
- **Agents**: what AI agents may do with this connection.

A **read-only** connection's sessions are read-only on the server, and AirSQL itself runs on it only statements it can
prove only read: SELECT, WITH … SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE and EXPLAIN (as [read-only queries](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html)
decide), and USE. Anything else is refused before it is sent, with the reason, from the query tab, the navigator, a
compare's sync script, Restore, Run SQL File and CSV import, so not even `SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ WRITE` can lift
it. A table tab's WHERE filter goes through the same check, within the whole SELECT it runs in, so a condition can't
call a function such as `SLEEP` or `GET_LOCK` there. Open in Terminal starts `mysql` with a read-only session. The
grid and the editors don't apply changes to it, and agents can't write to it either. The process list's Kill Query
and Kill Connection still work: they stop a statement or a connection and change no data.

**Test Connection** connects with what the editor shows, reports each hop with its time, and disconnects. **Save and
Connect** saves and connects; **Save** only saves.

## Routes

Every route but Direct ends in a private socket on this Mac, in a folder only you can open. AirSQL, the client tools
and Terminal all connect through it, so the route works the same for each.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| Direct | TCP to the host and port, or the server's own socket on this Mac. |
| SSH tunnel | ssh to the SSH host, which connects to the database host. |
| SSH through jump hosts | ssh through each jump host in order, then the SSH host. |
| SSH through a proxy | The first SSH host is reached through an HTTP CONNECT or SOCKS5 proxy (jump hosts optional). |
| Proxy, no SSH | The proxy connects to the database host itself. |

The database host is the name as the last SSH host or the proxy reaches it: often `127.0.0.1` or a private address.

SSH hosts log in with your ssh-agent and keys in `~/.ssh`, a key file, or a password. Whatever the server asks for
besides (a key's passphrase, a password, a code from your phone) appears as a question when you connect; tick
**Remember in Keychain** to save a password or passphrase once the connection works. The first time you reach an SSH
host, AirSQL shows its key fingerprint to trust; ssh remembers it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.

Your `~/.ssh/config` still applies: type one of its `Host` names as an SSH host and its settings (user, port, key,
its own proxy) are used, after what the editor sets.

## Import hosts from ~/.ssh/config

**File ▸ Import from ~/.ssh/config…** asks you to pick the file (it opens on `~/.ssh/config`), lists its hosts, and
makes a connection for each one you tick: an SSH tunnel through that host to a database on `127.0.0.1:3306`, which
you can then edit.

## Import and export connections

- **File ▸ New Connection from URL…** takes a `mysql://user@host:3306/database` address (or `mariadb://`), from the
  clipboard when it holds one, and opens the connection's settings to check before you save.
- **File ▸ Import Connections…** reads the saved connections of Sequel Ace, TablePlus, DBeaver or MySQL Workbench when
  they are on this Mac, or a file you choose: an AirSQL export, one of those apps' files, or HeidiSQL's exported
  settings. It lists the MySQL and MariaDB connections with ticks; one that is already here starts unticked.
- **File ▸ Export Connections…** saves the selected connections, or all of them, to a file for another Mac or a
  colleague.

Passwords never come along: an export has none, an import doesn't read them, and a password in a URL is left out.
AirSQL asks for each when you connect. An imported AirSQL file also leaves out what would run by itself: the client
programs chosen, startup SQL and agent access. TLS starts strict, except for a server on this Mac.

## Connect and disconnect

Double-click a connection (once it is connected, a double-click opens or closes its tree), or select it and choose
**Connection ▸ Connect** (⌘K). The status bar shows each step, hop
by hop, with Cancel. A connection that drops (the network goes away, the server restarts) is marked in the sidebar;
AirSQL never reconnects behind your back. **Connection ▸ Disconnect** (⇧⌘K) asks first when a tab has an open
transaction or edits that aren't applied.

Connected connections are kept alive with a ping every minute, except a session whose transaction has been open longer
than the safety setting allows.

## Folders

Folders group connections in the sidebar. **Connection ▸ New Folder…** makes one (the selected connections move into
it); right-click a folder to rename or delete it (its connections stay; Delete asks too). To move connections, drag them onto
a folder (or onto the list to take them out of one), or use **Connection ▸ Move to Folder**. Right-click the list's empty
space for New Connection and New Folder. F2 on a connection opens it to rename, and the filter's ↓ and Return go on to
the first match.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/navigator.html

# Browse a server

Once a connection is connected, the sidebar shows its databases under it. Each database groups its objects by kind:
tables, views, sequences (MariaDB), procedures, functions, triggers and events, with how many there are.

## Find your way

- **Click** a database to see its tables in the database view: rows, the space their data and indexes take, engine,
  collation, when they last changed and their comment. Click a column's title to sort by it; AirSQL keeps the order
  and the widths. **Filter by name** at its top keeps the tables with those letters. Right-click below the rows, or an
  empty database, for **Create Table…**.
- **Click** a table or view to see its rows; **double-click** it (or press Return) to open it in a tab of its own.
- **Click** a routine, trigger or event to see its definition; **double-click** (or **Open**) to open it in its editor.
- **Click the arrow** beside a table or view (or press →) to see what it holds without opening it: **Columns** with
  their types (the primary key's are marked **PK**), and for a table **Indexes**, **Foreign Keys**, **Checks** and
  **Triggers**. Hold the pointer over a row for all of it: a column's default, an index's columns, where a key points.
  **Double-click** a row to open the table's structure (a trigger, its editor); right-click a column for **Copy Name**,
  or drag it into the SQL editor. All of this comes from what AirSQL already read, so it asks the server nothing.
- **Open Structure** in a table's menu opens the table editor ([Change tables, views and routines](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html));
  **Create Table…** makes a table in the database you right-clicked; **New…** on a group (Tables, Views…) makes
  another of its kind.
- **Double-click** a database to make it the current one (it shows in bold, and in the toolbar's database pop-up) and
  open it; double-click again to close it. The console's statements run in the current database ([The SQL console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html)).
- **Right-click** anything for everything you can do with it; the tab in front stays. Every command is also in the
  **Database** menu. **Copy Name** quotes it for SQL, **Copy Name Without Quotes** doesn't, and **Copy CREATE** copies
  the statement that makes it.
- Hold ⌘ or ⇧ to select several tables, then drop, empty, check or change them all at once.
- Type a few letters of a name to jump to it, or type in the sidebar's filter (⌥⌘J) to show only what matches. While you
  filter, a connected connection whose name doesn't match shows the objects that do, opened.
- Drag a table, column or database into the SQL editor to insert its name, quoted for SQL.
- F2 renames the selected table or view (or folder), as **Database ▸ Rename…** does.
- **Refresh** (⌘R) reads the selected database or objects again from the server; with the connection selected, all of it.

On a server with more than 3,000 tables, AirSQL reads only the names when it connects; a database's columns, indexes and
keys load when you open it (a spinner shows on its row meanwhile). Change the number in Settings ▸ Connections.

## Change databases and tables

Every change shows its SQL first ([Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html)); nothing runs until you choose to.

- **New Database…** asks for a name, a character set and a collation (the server's own are chosen at first).
- **Drop…** deletes the selected databases or objects. Dropping a database always asks you to type its name; on a
  Production connection, so does dropping or emptying a table.
- **Truncate…** deletes every row of the selected tables. It can't be rolled back.
- **Rename…** gives a table or view a new name. Views and routines that use the old name aren't changed.
- **Copy Table…** copies a table into the same or another database, with its rows or without, or only the rows where a
  condition you type holds (for example `created_at >= '2026-01-01'`). Indexes come along; foreign keys don't.
- **Bulk Table Editor…** moves the selected tables to another database, or changes their engine, or converts them and
  their text columns to another character set and collation.
- **Maintenance** ▸ Analyze, Check, Optimize, Repair or Checksum runs on the selected tables and shows what the server
  said in a tab. Analyze, Optimize and Repair show their SQL first: Optimize rebuilds a table and locks it meanwhile.

A read-only connection offers none of these.

## Write SQL from the tree

These open a query tab with the SQL in it, built from the names AirSQL read; nothing runs until you press Run.

- **Generate SELECT**, **Generate INSERT** and **Generate UPDATE** on a table's or view's menu (in the sidebar or the
  database view) write a statement with its columns. A `?` marks each value for you to fill in: INSERT leaves out the
  columns the server fills itself (auto-increment and generated ones), and UPDATE finds the row by its primary key (or a
  unique key whose columns can't be NULL; without one, you write the condition).
- **Run…** on a procedure's menu writes its `CALL`, with a `?` and the name and type of each value it takes; OUT and
  INOUT parameters go in variables that a `SELECT` after the call shows. On a function's menu it writes a `SELECT` of it.
- **New Query**, **Export…** and **Restore…** on a database's menu start in that database.

## Find text on the server

**Find Text on Server…** looks for a text in every text column of every table (or of one database), and lists the
tables that hold it with how many rows. It reads each table in full, so it can take a while on a big server: the status
bar shows how far it is, and **Stop** or Cancel ends it. Double-click a table in the list, or press Return, to see its
matching rows; right-click it to open all its rows or copy its name. A column's header sorts the list.
Upper and lower case match as the column's collation says (most ignore case).

## See what the server is running

**Process List** (⌥⌘P, or **Processes** under the sidebar) lists every connection to the server and the statement it is
running, refreshed every 5 seconds (choose another interval, or Off). Click a column's title to sort by it (Time starts
with the longest running); type in **Filter** to keep the rows with those words, and tick **Hide Sleeping** to leave out
idle connections. Double-click a row (or press Return) to read its whole statement; Delete offers to kill it.

- **Kill Query…** stops a statement; its connection stays.
- **Kill Connection…** ends a connection, rolling back its open transaction.

Both ask first. Right before it stops anything, AirSQL checks that the process is still running what the list showed
(on MariaDB, that exact statement); if it has moved on, nothing is stopped and AirSQL says so. Both work on a
read-only connection too: they change no data.

## Getting back to your tabs

When you open AirSQL again, your tabs come back in their old order with the old one showing, and so does the sidebar's
selection. Query tabs are as you left them. Table, structure and process-list tabs come back as placeholders: AirSQL doesn't
connect to anything by itself, also not to a Production connection.

- A placeholder says what the tab was and where. **Connect and Open** connects the usual way, with its prompts, then
  loads the tab in the same place; on a connection that's connected already the button is **Open**, which just loads.
- If the connect fails, the tab stays and says why, with **Try Again**, **Edit Connection…** and **Troubleshooting**.
- A placeholder closes without a question, and Quit doesn't ask about it.
- Only names are kept: the connection, database, object and kind. Rows and filters aren't. Pending changes aren't part of
  the tab: they stay with the table and show when you [open it](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html).
- A tab whose connection you deleted doesn't come back.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html

# A table's rows

A table tab shows a table's or view's rows in the data grid. They load a page at a time from the connection's data
session, a session of their own, so a long query in a query tab never holds them up. Edits wait until you apply them.

## Load rows

- The first page loads when the tab opens: **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Rows per page** rows (1,000 at first), in the table's
  key order, so pages follow one another.
- The status bar says how many rows are loaded and of how many: `1,000 of about 52,000 rows`. The total is the server's
  estimate until you click **Count Exactly** (**Data ▸ Count Rows Exactly**), which runs `COUNT(*)` with the filter.
  An estimate below what has already loaded is left out (InnoDB's can say 0 of a million rows), and with no figure to go
  by, Load All and an unindexed sort ask first. After the count comes the time the rows were read: `· read 14:32`.
- **Load More** (⌥⌘↓) loads the next page; **Load All** (⌥⇧⌘↓) loads every row that's left, in batches as they arrive.
  Above **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Load All asks above** rows (100,000 at first) it asks first: every row is held in memory
  while the tab is open. Cancel it in the status bar's activity: what arrived stays, and Load More and Load All carry
  on from there.
- Anything slow here (a page, a filter, a sort, Load All, Count Exactly, Column Summary) can be stopped with **⌘.**, the
  toolbar's Cancel or the status bar's activity. A cancelled page leaves the rows as they were; Refresh (⌘R) loads them.
- Pages are read by offset. If someone adds or deletes rows between pages, a row can repeat or be missing: a notice says
  so when it happens, and Refresh reads the rows again.
- **View ▸ Refresh** (⌘R) reads the table's columns and loads the rows shown again; **View ▸ Refresh Every** does it by itself every 5 to 60 seconds,
  until you choose **Off**. Pending changes stay.

## Filter, search and sort

**Filter** and **Search** hide the rows that don't match; **Find** (⌘F) leaves every row and moves between matches.
**Find Text on Server** looks through every table, not only this one.

The chip at the left of the grid bar always says where filtering runs: **On server** (every row of the table, loaded or
not) or **Local** (only the rows loaded so far, at once, with no query).

- **Filter**: type a condition, as you would after WHERE, for example `status = 'paid' AND total > 100`, and press Return. A leading `WHERE` is
  fine. It is coloured as SQL, as in the query tab, and the field grows as the condition wraps, up to eight lines (then
  it scrolls); ⌥↩ starts a new line. Suggestions show as you type: columns, then operators,
  then the column's values (read from its first 10,000 rows), then AND and OR. ↑ and ↓ choose, Tab inserts, ⎋ closes, and
  ⌥⎋ brings them up anywhere. The clock (or ⌥↓ in the field) lists the table's last
  20 filters; the ⓧ, or **Data ▸ Clear Filter**, shows every row again. The filter and the sort are kept for the next
  time the table opens. On a read-only connection, the whole SELECT must pass the
  [read-only check](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html): a condition that calls a function such as `SLEEP` or `GET_LOCK` isn't sent,
  and the bar under it says why. The **?** at the bar's end opens [Read the data in a grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html).
- **Search all columns** (⇧⌘E) finds rows with the text in any column, as HeidiSQL does: text and JSON columns with
  `LIKE`, numbers and dates as text, binary columns by a whole `0x…` value. Tick **Loaded rows only** to search just the
  loaded rows instead.
- Search and `LIKE` read the text a cell shows, BIT digits and JSON included. Whether they ignore case is the column's
  collation: `utf8mb4_bin` and other binary ones don't, and JSON follows the connection's.
- **Quick Filter**: right-click a cell for `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `LIKE` (starts with, ends with, contains), `IS NULL` and
  `IS NOT NULL` with its value, and `IN` / `NOT IN` with every value selected in its column. Each item shows its SQL.
  Hold ⌥ to add the condition to the current filter with `AND`. The clipboard's text is offered too. **Data ▸ Quick
  Filter** has the same conditions by name (Less Than Selection, Contains Selection, In Selected Values…); ⌃⌘1 and ⌃⌘2
  filter by the focused cell's value, equal and not equal.
- **Type a Value…** (in both Quick Filter menus) asks for the value: choose how to compare (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, starts
  with, contains, ends with), type the value, and press **Filter**. Tick **Add to the current filter** to keep the
  filter there is and add the condition with `AND`.
- **Filter by Values…** (the funnel on a column's header, shown on hover and on a filtered column; **Data ▸ Filter by
  Values…**; or a header's menu): the column's values with how many rows have each, counted on the server within the
  current filter (the 1,000 most frequent). Tick the ones to show, or type part of a value and press **Contains**. The
  funnel opens over the rows and replaces its own earlier choice, so you can widen it again. In
  **Column Summary…**, a click on one of a column's most frequent values adds it to the filter.
- **Sort**: double-click a header, or click the arrow at its right, to sort by that column, ascending, then descending,
  then not at all. To sort by several columns, ⇧-click the next column's arrow (⌥ works too, and ⌥-double-click on a
  header), or right-click its header for **Add to Sort**; each arrow shows its place in the order. **Data ▸ Sort by
  Columns…** (or a header's menu) sets several at once: a line per
  column, each **Ascending** or **Descending**; the arrows move a column up or down the order, **Add Column** adds one
  and the minus takes it away. Rows sort on the server, and rows the sort leaves equal go in key order, so pages never
  repeat or miss a row (a view or a table without a key has no such order). On a table of over a million rows, sorting
  by a column without an index asks first (**Settings ▸ Safety**, on at first). With **Loaded rows only** ticked, the
  loaded rows sort here instead, as plain text without case or accents, or by value in number columns: the server's
  collation can order them otherwise, and an ENUM goes by its text.
- **Find** (⌘F) and **Find and Replace** (⌥⌘F) work on the loaded rows: ⌘G and ⇧⌘G go to the next and previous match,
  the bar says `3 of 12`, and every match is tinted, as are the cells Search All Columns found. **Options** has Match
  Case, Regular Expression (`$1` in the replacement), Whole Words and Filter Rows, which hides the loaded rows without a
  match. Replacements are pending edits, like any other.

## Edit rows

Nothing is written until you apply. Leaving a row writes nothing.

- **Edit a cell**: type over it, double-click it, or press Return or F2 (as in HeidiSQL). ⌫ starts with the cell empty.
  Return keeps the edit, Esc cancels, Tab moves to the next cell. Select several cells and type: each gets the value its column takes. Record View and Transpose edit
  the same way.
- **Values are checked as you keep them**, by the column's type and the server's sql_mode, as Apply will write them: a
  number too big for its column, a third decimal in `DECIMAL(10,2)`, a day the month doesn't have, a word that isn't
  one of an ENUM's. The editor then stays open and says why under the cell: fix the value or press Esc. Typing is never
  blocked, and numbers and DECIMAL travel as the text you typed, so nothing is rounded on the way.
- **Each type has its editor**:
  - BOOLEAN, TINYINT(1) and BIT(1) show a checkbox. Space, Return or a double click ticks or clears it; typing `t`,
    `f` or `n` sets true, false or NULL.
  - An ENUM shows its values in a list over the cell; a SET a checklist, where **Set** keeps the ticked ones. Typing
    still works: `read,write`.
  - Dates and times are typed as `YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss`, with fractional seconds when the column keeps them; ↑ and ↓
    step the part under the cursor (the day, the hour…). Zero dates are kept where sql_mode allows them, TIMESTAMP
    values are in the session's time zone, and a NULL cell starts empty: it never fills in today's date.
  - Bytes (BINARY, BLOB, shapes) are typed as hex: `0x00FF`. BIT shows and takes every bit: `b'1010'` or `1010`.
  - A value of more than 256 characters, or of several lines, opens in the value panel (below).
  - A foreign key shows the rows of the table it refers to, each as "label (key)", the label being that table's
    first text column, or the one you chose with **Use as Label** (below). They are searched on the server as you
    type, by label or by key, 100 at a time, so a big table is never listed whole. Return or a double click puts the
    key in the cell. **Data ▸ Choose Referenced Row…** opens the same list.
- **The value panel** (⇧↩) edits the selected cell too: ⌘↩ or clicking elsewhere keeps the text as a pending edit,
  Esc puts the cell's value back. A value the column refuses stays there, and the panel says why. Its **⋯** menu has
  **Format JSON** and **Compact JSON**, **Load from File…** (a file's bytes in a binary column, else its UTF-8 text)
  and **Save to File…**.
- **Data ▸ Insert Value** (and a cell's right-click menu) puts in a value the server works out when Apply runs:
  `NULL`, `DEFAULT`, `NOW()`, `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`, `CURDATE()`, `CURTIME()`, `UNIX_TIMESTAMP()`, `UUID()`, `UUID_SHORT()`
  or a random value, whichever fit the column. Until then the cell shows it in grey: `ƒ NOW()`.
- **Data ▸ Add Row** (⌘I) adds a new row after the loaded ones. Where the server fills a value in, the new row says so
  in grey: *auto* (AUTO_INCREMENT), *default*, *generated*. **Duplicate Row** (⌘D) copies the selected rows, and
  their AUTO_INCREMENT columns show *auto* for the server to number; **Duplicate Row Without Keys** (⇧⌘D) leaves every
  key column to the server too.
  **Delete Rows** (⌘⌫, or ⌫ on rows selected by their numbers) marks the selected rows for deletion. **Cut** (⌘X) copies
  the selected cells and clears them: NULL where the column allows it, else empty. **Set NULL** (⌥⌘N) and **Set DEFAULT** set the selected
  cells.
- **Edit ▸ Paste** (⌘V) puts cells copied from Excel, Numbers or a grid (tab-separated, or CSV) into the cells from the
  selected one on, as pending edits: numbers with a comma for decimals and dates such as `31.12.2026` or `12/31/2026`
  are read the way the column's values are written. Rows past the last loaded one become new rows, and one value pasted
  over several selected cells fills them all. Cells that can't go in their column are listed first, so you can paste
  the others or nothing. **Data ▸ Paste as New Rows** adds every copied row as a new one. A cell reading `NULL` (the
  grid's NULL text) is NULL.
- When the copied cells could be read two ways, the **Paste Format** sheet asks first, starting from AirSQL's guess:
  what separates the cells (lines of commas or semicolons without tabs may be CSV), the decimal mark (numbers such as
  `1,234`), and the order of day, month and year (dates such as `03/04/2026`). **Data ▸ Paste with Format…** always
  asks.
- **Data ▸ Related Rows** (⌃⌘↓) lists the row a foreign key cell points to and the rows of other tables that point to
  the selected row; choosing one opens that table filtered to them.

### Foreign key labels and virtual foreign keys

- A one-column foreign key's cell shows the row it refers to in grey after its value (before it, for a number): the
  referenced table's label, read from the server for the rows on screen only. Right-click a column header of the
  referenced table and choose **Use as Label** (also in the Data menu) to show that column instead of its first text
  column; choose it again to go back.
- Many schemas have no real foreign keys. Right-click a column header and choose **Add Virtual Foreign Key…** to say
  which table's key the column holds (AirSQL guesses from the name: `customer_id` → `customers`). AirSQL keeps it on
  this Mac with the table's view settings, never in the database. The drop-down, Related Rows (both ways), the labels
  and the [ER diagram](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html#the-er-diagram) then follow it as a real foreign key. **Remove Virtual Foreign Key**
  forgets it.
- Pending changes have their colours: an edited cell amber, a new row green, a row to delete struck through in red.
  The bar under the grid bar counts them.
- **Undo** (⌘Z) and **Redo** (⇧⌘Z) step through the pending changes (a paste or a multi-cell edit is one step);
  **Revert** (⌥⌘Z) discards the selected rows' changes, **Revert All** every one.
- Pending changes are kept on disk as you make them. If AirSQL quits or the Mac restarts, they come back the next time
  you open the table, marked "Kept from before".
- Closing the tab with pending changes asks whether to keep them for later or throw them away. Quitting AirSQL lists,
  in one sheet, the tables with pending changes and any transaction still open in a query tab (which is rolled back).

### Which tables can be edited

AirSQL addresses each row by its primary key, or, without one, by the first unique key whose columns can't be NULL. Key
values are never shortened, so a change always reaches exactly its row. A table with neither is read-only, and the bar
says why; so are views. Generated columns can't be edited.

## Apply changes

- A table a single click shows, in the preview tab, keeps its pending changes when you click another table: the tab
  stays open with its dot, and the next table gets a preview of its own.
- **Data ▸ Apply Changes** (⌘S) writes every pending change in one transaction on the data session: deletes first (in
  batches of 500), then edits, then new rows. Each edit's `UPDATE` names the row by its key and the edited cells by the
  values you loaded (`` `price` <=> 10 ``), and each statement must change exactly its rows. If one changes another
  number (someone else changed a cell you edited, or deleted the row, since it was loaded) or the server refuses one,
  everything is rolled back, nothing is applied, and the grid selects the row; when the server's error names a column
  ("Data too long for column 'note'", "Column 'name' cannot be null", a duplicate value of a unique key), it selects
  that cell. Fix the value and apply again; if someone else got there first, revert the change, reload the rows and
  make it again. Changes kept over a restart are checked the same way.
- **Manual Commit** (the toolbar's transaction pop-up, or Query ▸ Transaction Mode) moves the table tab to a session of its
  own. Each Apply then writes into a transaction left open, and the rows you read show those changes, until **Commit** or
  **Roll Back**. Each Apply is still all or nothing. Closing the tab or quitting with the transaction open asks first.
- What Apply can't check: FLOAT, TIMESTAMP, JSON, spatial and vector values, dates with a zero month or day and values
  over 64 KB don't compare exactly, so edits to those go by the key alone and overwrite what is there; the preview
  names them. A change that only differs in case or trailing spaces can pass on a column whose collation ignores
  those. Rows to delete go by their key: someone else's change to a row doesn't stop its delete, and neither does a
  change to a column you didn't edit stop your edit.
- **Preview SQL…** shows the statements first, in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html). The preview also comes first on
  connections where **Settings ▸ Safety ▸ Show the SQL before the grid's Apply** is on (every Production connection),
  and whenever there is a warning: a table on MyISAM, Aria, MEMORY or another engine that can't roll back, or deletes
  that also change other tables through `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `SET NULL`.
- Values are checked again as Apply writes them; one that no longer fits (sql_mode changed, or it came from a find
  and replace) stops Apply before anything runs, and the grid selects its cell.
- After Apply, new rows stay where they were and show what the server filled in, their AUTO_INCREMENT key (the insert
  ID) and defaults included: each is read back by its key. When every row of the table (or of the filter) is loaded,
  the edited rows are read back by their keys and the deleted ones go, so nothing else loads again; otherwise the
  loaded rows load again. A new row's untouched cell shows **auto**, **default** or **generated**, in the value panel
  too, until Apply.

## Copy and export

These work in a query's results too.

- **Edit ▸ Copy** (⌘C) copies the selected cells in the format last chosen in **Copy As** (TSV at first); in a query tab
  result with nothing selected, every row. **Copy with Headers** (⌥⌘C) puts the column names first. Values are copied
  whole, as stored, whatever **Display As** shows. **View ▸ View As ▸ Text** shows the rows in the same format.
- **Edit ▸ Copy As** ▸ TSV, CSV, JSON, JSON Lines, Markdown, HTML Table, XML, SQL INSERT, INSERT IGNORE, REPLACE,
  UPDATE, DELETE or WHERE Clause. The SQL formats address rows by the key, and UPDATE and DELETE add any of it you
  didn't copy; without a key, by every column copied. The one you choose becomes ⌘C's format.
- **Data ▸ Export Rows…** (and a result tab's **Export Result…**) saves the selected rows, the loaded rows (with their
  pending changes) or every row of the table with its filter and sort, streamed from the server on a session of its own, as CSV, TSV, JSON, JSON Lines, SQL,
  Markdown, HTML, XML or an Excel workbook (.xlsx). Choose whether the column names come first, how NULL is written
  (`NULL`, `\N` or nothing) and Windows line endings, then **Export…** to a file or **Copy** to the clipboard.
  In a workbook, exact numbers over 15 digits (a 20-digit id, a long DECIMAL) go as text, as Excel would round them,
  and a value over Excel's 32,767 characters a cell is cut: AirSQL says how many were, and CSV keeps them whole.
  Hidden columns aren't exported, and the sheet says how many are left out. SQL formats leave out generated columns.
  In CSV a real NULL has no quotes and the text NULL has them, so CSV import tells them apart; TSV has no way to.
  CSV is UTF-8 without a BOM, which scripts read as it is: Excel for Mac needs **Data ▸ From Text**.
  XML and HTML can't hold control characters, nor can a workbook: each shows as �.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html

# Read the data in a grid

A table's rows and a query's results show in the same grid. These parts of it help you read what is there: the
status bar's figures, the value panel, Record View, Transpose, other ways to show a column, colours, text, charts, and
a column's summary. Loading, filtering, editing, copying and exporting a table's rows are on
[A table's rows](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html).

## The header

Each column's header shows its name and, under it, its type. Marks before the name tell you about keys:

- a gold key: the primary key, or the unique key the grid uses to find a row when there is no primary key;
- a 1 in a circle: another unique key; an outline key: an index;
- a chain link: a foreign key.

After the type, **auto** marks an auto-increment column, **generated** a generated one, **default** a column with a
default value, and **null** a column that allows NULL. Hold the pointer over a header for all of this in words and the
column's comment.

## The status bar

With cells selected, the status bar shows the focused cell (**r3 : c5**, row and column), how many cells are
selected, and one figure for them: their sum, or their count when they aren't numbers. Click the figure to see them
all (count, sum, average, smallest, largest, median, distinct values) and choose the one shown. Sums of decimals are
exact; a whole column's figure says **of loaded rows** while the table has more. Only whole numbers add up: dates,
version numbers, phone numbers and BIT values get a count. **Edit ▸ Copy Selection Summary** (⇧⌘C) copies every figure.
Selections of more than 100,000 cells aren't added up. In a narrow window the figure, then the focused cell, make way for the rest; a table's row count and its **Count
Exactly**, **Load More** and **Load All** stay. Right-click them to copy what they say, or to count or load rows.

## Move around

- **Data ▸ Go to Row…** (⌘L) goes to a row by its number, or to `column:row`, the column by its name or number:
  `email:120`.
- **View ▸ Column List…** (⌘J) lists every column. Type to find one; Return (or a double-click) jumps to it; its box,
  or Space, shows or hides it; **Show All** brings back hidden columns.
- **Edit ▸ Extend Selection** (⌥↑) grows the selection from the focused cell to its column, then its row, then
  everything; **Shrink Selection** (⌥↓) goes back the same way.
- Hold ⇧ to scroll a mouse wheel across, and ⌥ to scroll five times as far.
- **Data ▸ Hide Column** hides the selected columns. A column comes back where it was.
- **Data ▸ Freeze** keeps the columns up to the focused one (the key column, say) at the left while you scroll across.
  Choose it on the last frozen column to unfreeze them. AirSQL remembers it for each table.
- Esc closes the find bar, leaves Record View and Transpose, then narrows the selection to the focused cell.
- Drag a header to move its column, drag its right edge to resize it, and double-click the edge to fit its values.
  AirSQL remembers the columns' order, widths, hidden and frozen columns and display types for each table, and for
  each query in the query tab, so they open as you left them.
- **View ▸ Bigger** (⌘+) and **Smaller** (⌘−) change the grid's text size while it has the focus; **Actual Size** (⌘0)
  goes back to the size in Settings ▸ Grid.

## See a whole value

- **View ▸ Value Panel** (⇧↩) opens the focused cell's whole value beside the grid, never shortened: as wrapped text,
  as a JSON tree, as hex, or as a picture when the bytes are an image. It follows the cell you select. A double-click
  on a cell you can't edit opens it too.
- **View ▸ Record View** (⌥⌘R) shows the focused row as a form, a line per column. **Previous** and **Next** above it
  (or **View ▸ Previous Record** ⌥⌘← and **Next Record** ⌥⌘→) move between rows; **Back to the Grid** returns. A double-click
  on a row's number opens it. In a table, its values can be edited there as in the grid. A filter or a sort on a
  query result shows the grid again, as does an Apply that deletes the row.
- **View ▸ Transpose** (⌥⌘T, the grid's right-click menu, or the button at the end of a table's grid bar) turns rows
  into columns, with the column names down the left: handy for comparing a few wide rows. A query result with one row opens this way; **Settings ▸ Grid ▸ Transpose results with one row** turns
  that off. Transpose shows the first 1,000 rows.

## Show a column another way

**Data ▸ Display As** (also on a cell's right-click menu) changes how the selected columns look, not what they hold:
copying and editing use the stored value.

- Numbers: **Number with Grouping**; **Decimal Places ▸** rounds them (half up) to none, 1, 2, 3 or 4 decimal places,
  grouped by thousands as your Mac groups them; or **Date from Unix Time** (seconds or milliseconds), in your time zone.
- Dates: **Short**, **Medium** or **Long Date and Time**, as your Mac writes dates (System Settings ▸ General ▸ Language
  & Region). A DATE column shows the date only. Zero dates, TIME and YEAR stay as stored.
- A TIMESTAMP cell's tooltip names the session's time zone, which the value is shown in.
- **Time Zone ▸** (DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns) moves the values: **From UTC to This Mac's** takes them as UTC and
  shows them in your time zone; **From This Mac's to UTC** does the reverse. A TIMESTAMP arrives in the session's time
  zone, so choose the first one when that is UTC. The header says so (`datetime as medium date, UTC → this Mac's`).
- Bytes: **UUID** (for `binary(16)`), **Hex**, or **Text (UTF-8)**.
- **As Stored** shows the value as the server sent it again. AirSQL remembers each column's choice for each table.

## Colours

- **View ▸ Heatmap** colours the selected number columns by value, pale for the smallest and strong for the largest.
  A column with negative and positive numbers is red below zero and green above; one of only 0 and 1 marks the 1s.
  With everything selected (⌘A), every number column gets one. Choose it again to take it away.
- **View ▸ Highlight Equal Values** tints every cell holding the focused cell's value.
- What a colour marks is said too: with VoiceOver, a cell says **changed**, **added** or **removed** after its column's
  name, for pending changes and for a comparison's rows, and a compared cell's help gives the other side's value.

## Text, tree and charts

- **View ▸ View As ▸ Text** shows the rows as text in the copy format (**Edit ▸ Copy As**: TSV at first, or CSV, JSON,
  Markdown, SQL INSERT…), with the column names; **Tree** shows them as JSON, a row per item, with JSON columns opened
  up. **Table** goes back. Both show the first 10,000 rows. In a tree (here or in the value panel), double-click an
  object or array to open or close it; right-click to copy a value or to open or close every one.
- **View ▸ Chart** draws the rows as a bar, line, area, pie, scatter or histogram chart of a number column, by another
  column. Choose the kind and columns above the chart; point at it to read a value. Bars add up the values of each
