  label and show the first 30 labels; a pie shows eight slices and puts the rest in **Other**. Lines, areas and points
  by a date column go in date order along a date axis; by a text column, along the row numbers. A chart covers the
  first 10,000 rows of those loaded, and under it, and in its picture, says so when that leaves rows out. **Save as
  PNG…** saves a picture of it. Pie charts need macOS 14 or later.

## Column Summary

**Data ▸ Column Summary…** (also on a header's right-click menu) counts the focused column's distinct values and NULLs,
finds its smallest and largest values, and lists its 50 most frequent values with how often each appears. For a table
the server works this out over all its rows within the filter; it asks first when the table is larger than 2 GB.
Click a value to show only the rows that hold it (it is added to the filter). For a query result it counts the rows
you have.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html

# Change tables, views and routines

AirSQL edits a table's structure in a form, and views, procedures, functions, triggers and events as the CREATE
statement that makes them. Nothing changes on the server until you apply, and the SQL that will run is always shown
first.

## The table editor

Open it from a table's **Open Structure**, or make a new table with **Database ▸ Create Table…**. A table editor has five
parts, chosen at the top:

- **Columns**: name, type (the types your server has), length or ENUM values, unsigned, NULL, default, extra (counts up
  by itself, follows updates, or is generated from an expression), collation and comment. Drag rows to reorder the
  columns.
- **Indexes**: primary key, unique, plain, full-text and spatial indexes. Write their columns separated by commas:
  `email(10)` indexes the first 10 characters, `created_at DESC` sorts down.
- **Foreign keys**: this table's columns, the table they point at and its columns, and what happens on update and on
  delete.
- **Checks**: conditions every row must satisfy. On MariaDB, a check written with a column belongs to that column and
  stays with it when the column changes.
- **Options**: the table's name, engine, default collation, row format, next AUTO_INCREMENT number and comment.

**+** adds a row, **−** removes the selected rows (or press Delete), and a right-click offers the same. New rows show in
green and changed ones in amber until you apply. **Edit ▸ Undo** takes back a change; **Revert** takes back all of them.
Drag columns to put them in another order, or press ⇧⌘↑ and ⇧⌘↓. ⌘C copies the selected rows as the lines of a CREATE TABLE; ⌘V in this list, here or in another table's editor, adds them
as new rows.

Under the lists, the SQL that Apply would run updates as you type. When something can't work yet (a VARCHAR without a
length, two columns of one name, an emoji in a name, which the server would keep as `?`), it says what to fix instead.

## Apply

**Apply** (⌘S) shows the statements in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html) first. Then they run one at a time on a
connection of their own, and the editor reads the table back from the server.

- MySQL and MariaDB can't roll table changes back: each statement takes effect as it runs. When there are several, the
  preview says so; if one fails, the ones before it stay done, and the editor shows what is left to do.
- A changed foreign key is dropped in a statement of its own first: neither server takes a drop and an add of the same
  key in one statement.
- Dropping a column deletes its values, and changing a column's type converts them: the preview warns about both.
- A large table may be copied while it changes, and writes to it wait until that is done.

## Views, procedures, functions, triggers and events

Open one from the tree, or start a new one from **Database ▸ New Object**. The editor shows its CREATE statement, as the
server keeps it, to edit as text.

- **Runs as** chooses its DEFINER: the account it was created with, or you. Keeping another account's DEFINER needs the
  SET_USER_ID privilege on MySQL, or SET USER on MariaDB.
- Apply runs it in its database, under the sql_mode it was created with (and an event under its time zone), so it
  behaves as before. The footer shows those settings.
- MariaDB replaces it in one statement (CREATE OR REPLACE). MySQL replaces a view the same way, but drops a procedure,
  function, trigger or event first: if the new code fails, the old one is gone. Your code stays in the editor to fix and
  apply again, and **Revert** puts the old code back.
- The code has the tab's editor: line numbers, completion, Comment Lines (⌘/), Format SQL and the matching bracket.
- When the server refuses the code, the place it points to is underlined in red, with the message on hover, until you
  change the text.
- Renaming it in the code makes the new one and then drops the old one.

## The ER diagram

**Database ▸ ER Diagram** draws a database's tables with their keys. Tables that point at nothing come first on the left,
and each table sits right of the tables its foreign keys point at; lines go from a key's column to the table it points
at, virtual foreign keys you added in a table's rows included ([Virtual foreign keys](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/table-data.html#foreign-key-labels-and-virtual-foreign-keys)).
Tables with no keys come last.

Click a table to select it (the arrow keys move between tables), double-click it to open it in the table editor, and
right-click it for **Open Structure**, **Open Data** and **Copy Name** (⌘C copies the selected table's name too), or the empty space to export. Pinch,
⌘+ and ⌘− zoom, ⌘0 goes back to actual size and **Fit** shows the whole diagram; ⌘F goes to the find field, where typing
part of a name selects that table and Return goes to the next. ⌘R reads the schema again. **Export Image…** saves the diagram as a PNG, and **Export
Mermaid…** as Mermaid text, which many docs sites and wikis draw.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html

# Export, restore, copy and import

AirSQL backs up and moves data with your own `mysqldump` and `mysql` (or MariaDB's `mariadb-dump` and `mariadb`)
when you have them, and with its own code when you don't. Every command here is in the **Tools** and **File** menus
and in a connection's right-click menu in the sidebar.

## Which programs AirSQL uses

**Settings ▸ Client Tools** shows the programs AirSQL found and their versions. It looks in Homebrew's folders
(`/opt/homebrew/opt/mysql-client/bin` and the like, on Apple silicon and Intel), `/usr/local/mysql/bin` (MySQL's
installer), MAMP and your `PATH`. Leave the fields empty and AirSQL picks, for each server, the tools of its family
(MariaDB's for MariaDB, MySQL's for MySQL) closest to its version. Choose a program to always use that one.

A `.csv` dropped on the window or the Dock icon opens Import CSV with the file chosen, and a `.sql.gz` opens Run SQL
File the same way; nothing runs until you press the sheet's button.

Export, Restore, Run SQL File, Copy to Another Server and Import CSV each open in a window of their own, which you can
move aside to keep working. Closing it while it runs asks first; disconnecting the connection it uses, or quitting, says
it is running and stops it.

Each window says how well its tool suits the server: **✓ suits the server**, a warning (another family's tool, or an
older version than the server), or why it can't be used (not there, too old: AirSQL needs MySQL 5.7 or MariaDB 10.3
tools or newer). The tool you pick in one is remembered for that connection: it shows, and can be changed, in the
connection editor's Options tab.

No tools at all? Install MySQL's or MariaDB's client tools (for example `brew install mysql-client`), then choose
**Find Again**. Until then, Export and Run SQL File use AirSQL's own code.

## Export a database

**Tools ▸ Export…** (or right-click a connection ▸ Export…).

1. Tick the databases or tables to export. Space ticks the selected rows; right-click for Include All, Include None and
   Include Only These. The filter above the list shows only the tables with that text, each on its own line, so ticks
   reach only what you see; what's ticked stays ticked when you clear it. One database exports without `CREATE DATABASE`, so you can restore it under any name; several
   databases export whole, each with its own name.
2. Choose the content (structure and data, structure only, data only) and the options: one consistent snapshot
   (`--single-transaction`), binary as hex, gzip, `DROP TABLE` before each table, and views, routines, triggers and
   events.
3. Pick the tool (**Choose…** beside it finds a `mysqldump` or `mariadb-dump` anywhere on this Mac, and Restore and Run
   SQL File take a `mysql` or `mariadb` the same way), where to save the file, and any extra options of your own (`--skip-comments`, `--where=…`).
4. The box under the form shows the exact command line of the tool you picked, and **Copy Command** copies it. AirSQL's
   built-in export runs no command, so the box says what it does and the button isn't there.
5. **Export**. The window shows the table being written, the bytes so far and the time left. **Stop** ends it.

The dump goes into a hidden file next to the one you chose and takes its name only when it is complete, so a stopped
or failed export never leaves half a file. When it is done, **Show in Finder** shows you the file.

**AirSQL (built in)** in the Tool menu writes the SQL itself, through a connection of its own: the tables' `CREATE`
statements, their rows as `INSERT`s (binary as hex), then views, routines, triggers and events, all read in one
consistent snapshot. Its files restore with `mysql` or with Run SQL File.

## Restore a dump, or run a .sql file

**Tools ▸ Restore…** runs a `.sql` or `.sql.gz` file with your `mysql` or `mariadb`; **File ▸ Run SQL File…** opens the
same sheet with AirSQL's own runner, which splits the file into statements as `mysql` does (`DELIMITER` included) and
runs them one at a time. Compressed files are read through `/usr/bin/gzip`.

1. Choose the file and the database it runs in.
2. Choose what happens on an error: stop at the first one (what ran before it stays), or go on and count them
   (`--force`).
3. **Restore** (or **Run**).

Before anything runs, AirSQL reads the whole file for the statements that decide where it writes: `USE`,
`CREATE DATABASE`, `DROP DATABASE`, and `SET GTID_PURGED`. When the file switches to another database than the one you
chose, drops a database, or sets GTID_PURGED, or when the database it writes to has tables already, the SQL preview
sheet says so and asks first (Settings ▸ Safety ▸ *Ask before Restore…*). On a production connection it always asks.
Progress is the share of the file read, so it is real for compressed files too.

## Copy to another server

**Tools ▸ Copy to Another Server…** copies databases or tables straight from one connection to another, through a
session on each: no file in between.

- **To** and **Database**: the connection and the database the copy goes into (made if it isn't there). One database
  can take another name; views and routines follow the new name.
- **Replace tables that are there** drops the other server's tables of the same name first. It is off unless you tick
  it, and the SQL preview asks before it runs. Copies to a production connection always ask.
- If a statement fails, the copy stops; what was copied before it stays.

## Import a CSV file

**File ▸ Import CSV…**

1. Choose the file. AirSQL guesses the separator (comma, semicolon, tab or bar) and shows each field's first value.
2. Choose the table. Each column takes a field of the file, matched by name when the first row names the columns, by
   position when it doesn't, or **Leave out** to take its default.
3. **Import**. The rows go in one transaction: if one fails (a duplicate key, a value the column refuses), none of the
   file stays, and the message says which records.

Empty fields and a `NULL` without quotes become NULL unless you untick it (AirSQL's own CSV writes the text NULL in
quotes, so the two come back apart), and a whole `0x…` field in a BLOB or BINARY column becomes its bytes. The file should
be UTF-8: a field that isn't reads as Windows-1252, and the end of the import says so, as it does when the server gave
warnings. AirSQL sends the rows as `INSERT`s: `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` stays off.

## Open the mysql command line in Terminal

**Tools ▸ Open in Terminal** opens Terminal running `mysql` (or `mariadb`) on the connection, in its database. On a
[read-only connection](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html#add-or-edit-a-connection) it starts with `SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, as
AirSQL's own sessions do, so a slip can't change anything there. Exports get it too, where the dump tool knows how
(MySQL 8.4's and later); restores, Run SQL File, CSV import and copies into a read-only connection are refused.

## Your password stays private

The client tools get the login from a temporary option file that only you can read (file mode 0600, in a private
folder in AirSQL's Application Support folder), passed as `--defaults-file`, so `~/.my.cnf` and `/etc/my.cnf` don't
change where they connect. The password is never on the command line, in the environment, or in the command shown.
AirSQL removes the file as soon as the tool has read it: once a dump has started writing, once a restore is reading
its input, ten seconds after Terminal starts `mysql`; and anything left behind at the next launch.

Over TCP the tools check TLS the way the connection asks: MySQL's with `--ssl-mode`, MariaDB's with `--ssl` and
`--ssl-verify-server-cert`. A tool never runs without its certificate check. A certificate you trusted (pinned) is
checked by MariaDB tools that take `--ssl-fp`, which get its fingerprint; AirSQL asks the tool's `--help` whether it
does. Other tools run on such a connection only if it has a CA file and checks the authority, against that file.
MySQL's tools check certificates only against a CA file. When the tool can't check the server, the window says what
to do and **Use AirSQL's Built-in** switches to AirSQL's own export or runner, which check it as AirSQL does; such a
tool is never picked for you.

With a certificate you trusted and no CA file, Export, Restore and Run SQL File also offer MySQL's tools an unticked
box, **Run without checking the certificate**. The connection is encrypted but can't prove it's this server, so the
login and the dump could be exposed, and a restore's data goes to a server that isn't proved. The tool then runs with
`--ssl-mode=REQUIRED`, never without TLS; the tick lasts one run, is never saved, clears when you change the tool, and
the run is noted in the SQL log. MariaDB's older tools don't get the box, as without a check they can't insist on TLS.
Open in Terminal follows the same rules with an alert each time instead of a box: **Cancel** is the default, and **Open
Without Checking** goes on with TLS required, saving nothing. Copy to Another Server needs neither: it uses no client
tool, and AirSQL's own sessions check the certificate on both sides.

Client tools reach SSH and proxy routes through the connection's private socket once AirSQL is connected through them.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html

# Compare two databases

**Tools ▸ Compare…** (or **Compare…** in a connection's or a database's menu, which starts from it) opens a window
that compares two databases, on the same server or on two different connections, such as production against staging
or MySQL 8 against MariaDB. A connection that isn't connected connects when you choose it, asking for a password or
to trust a certificate on the compare window as the main window would; each side then works through its own route, on
a session of its own. The compare only reads; nothing changes until you run the sync script yourself.

## Run a compare

1. Choose the **source** on the left and the **target** on the right: a connection, then one of its databases (or
   type its name). The sync script makes the target like the source; **Swap** turns them around.
2. Choose what to compare: **Structure and Data**, **Structure** or **Data**.
3. Click **Compare** (⌘R). The bar under the setup shows the table and chunk being checked, and **Cancel** (⌘.)
   stops the compare; the statement running on each server is stopped too. The work is also listed in the main
   window's activity list.

The summary says how many tables match, differ in structure, or are only on one side, how many rows differ, and how
much of the data had to come over the network. The list shows what differs first: **only source** and **only target**
for objects on one side, **structure**, **data**, then **match**. The filter above it narrows it by name, and **Hide
Matching** leaves only what differs. Click an object to see it; double-click it, or press Return, to see its rows when
they differ. The two definitions scroll together.

## What is compared

- **Structure:** tables (columns, indexes, foreign keys, checks, engine, comment), views, procedures, functions,
  triggers, events and sequences. The **Structure** tab shows both definitions side by side, the lines only one
  side has marked.
- **Data:** the rows of every table both sides have, matched on the primary key, or on a unique key whose columns
  are all NOT NULL. The **Data** tab shows the rows that differ in the [data grid](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/data-grid.html), as a sync would
  change the target: rows only in the source in green (the script inserts them), rows only in the target in red and
  struck through (it deletes them), then rows in both whose differing cells are amber (it updates them); hold the
  pointer over an amber cell to see both values. The line above the rows counts each kind. The grid works as
  elsewhere: select cells or rows with ⌘ and ⇧, copy them in any format (⌘C, **Copy with Headers**, **Copy As**),
  sort by a header, see a long value in the value panel, or save the rows with **Export Rows…**. Tables without such a
  key are still checked as a whole, but their rows can't be matched or synced. Generated columns are left out: their
  values follow from the others.

MySQL and MariaDB write the same thing differently, and the compare reads them alike: `int(11)` and `int`, MariaDB's
JSON (a LONGTEXT with a check) and MySQL's, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `current_timestamp()`, `NO ACTION` and
`RESTRICT`, check constraints the two servers name differently. Each flavour writes a view's or routine's body its own
way, though (MariaDB adds `COLLATE` to a function's `RETURNS`), so the same one on MySQL and on MariaDB can still show as
different.

### Ignore rules

**Ignore Rules** chooses differences the compare doesn't count. All four are on at first:

- **AUTO_INCREMENT Values**: tables' next AUTO_INCREMENT values.
- **DEFINER**: who views, routines, triggers and events run as. The script then leaves DEFINER out, so they run as
  whoever runs the script.
- **Collations and Character Sets** of tables and columns (MySQL 8 and MariaDB have different defaults).
- **Whitespace in Definitions**: spaces and line breaks in bodies, outside quoted text.

### Tables…

**Tables…** lists the source's tables, once a source and database are chosen, so a long first compare can be limited.
Untick a table to leave it out, give the target table it should be compared with when it was renamed there, list
columns whose values shouldn't count (such as `updated_at`), or add a WHERE condition for its rows on both sides. Type
in the filter to find a table; **Compare All** and **Compare None** tick and untick the tables shown. Double-click a
table to tick or untick it, or right-click the selected tables (⌘ and ⇧ select several) for Compare and Leave Out. **Leave Out of Next Compare** in an object's menu unticks it
too.

## How the data compare stays fast

Each server sums up the rows of a chunk of the table (10,000 rows by key order) as a row count and a total of 64-bit
row hashes, computed from MD5. Only a chunk whose sums differ is looked at more closely: it is split into smaller
chunks, and for the small ones that still differ each row's key and hash come over, then only the rows that differ.
A million identical rows are checked without fetching any.

The hashes tell apart values that careless checksums mix up: a NULL and an empty string, values moved from one column
to another, `'a'` and `'A'` or `'a '` under a case-insensitive collation, the same text in latin1 and utf8mb4 (which
counts as the same). Both sessions use time zone `+00:00`, so TIMESTAMP values compare by the moment they stand for.
Floats, decimals written with another scale and JSON with other spacing or key order are compared as values.

## The sync script

The **Sync script** box shows the statements for the selected object; **Copy Sync Script** copies them. **Sync
Script…** opens the whole script in a [console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html) tab of the target named “Sync script”, to read (it can't
be edited there; **Save As…** keeps a copy). It never runs on its own: **Run** in that tab brings the compare window
back with the script in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html), where you can copy it, run it on the target, or cancel. It
runs:

1. `USE` the target database and `SET time_zone = '+00:00'`;
2. the structure changes, in order: foreign keys and objects that go or change are dropped first, then new tables,
   `ALTER TABLE`, views (after the views they use), foreign keys, routines, triggers and events. MySQL and MariaDB
   commit each structure change on its own: they can't be rolled back;
3. the row changes in one transaction: DELETE (children before parents), then UPDATE and INSERT (parents first). Each
   statement must change exactly the rows it names; if one doesn't, because the target changed since the compare,
   everything in the transaction is rolled back. Tables on MyISAM, Aria or MEMORY can't roll back, and the preview
   warns about them.

**Destructive steps are left out** unless you tick **Include destructive steps**: dropping tables, columns, indexes,
checks, foreign keys and other objects only the target has, deleting rows only the target has, and column changes
that could cut or refuse values (a shorter type, NOT NULL). Each destructive statement is marked with a
`-- Destructive:` comment, and the preview's button turns red.

Rows of tables only in the source come with their `CREATE TABLE`. New columns of existing tables get their default
values: after running the script, compare again to copy their values. After a sync, AirSQL offers to compare again.

**Save as Changeset…** saves the script as [Liquibase](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html) changesets in a changelog you choose; so does
**Query ▸ Save as Changeset…** in the “Sync script” tab.

## Compare two results, or a result with a table

In a [console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html), **Compare With…** (a result tab's right-click menu, or **Query ▸ Compare With…**) compares
the result shown with another one, row by row:

- **Compare with** offers the other result tabs of the window, this tab's nearest first (a result from another
  query tab, such as the same query on another server, carries that tab's name), then the tables and views of the tab's database.
- **Match rows on** says which columns tell rows apart: the result's key when it has one, a single column, or every
  column (rows then differ only as being on one side). Rows with the same values there are the same row; when several
  share them, they pair up in the order they come.
- The rows that differ open in a result tab of their own, named after the other side (“vs Yesterday”), next to the
  result: rows only in this result green, rows only in the other red and struck through, and in rows on both sides the
  cells that differ amber (hold the pointer over one to see both values). The results bar says how many rows are the
  same. When nothing differs, AirSQL says so instead.

Only the columns both sides have, by name, are compared, with the rules of the data compare: numbers, decimals of
another scale and floats as numbers, JSON as values (MySQL writes it its own way), NULL apart from an empty string. A
table is read up to 100,000 rows; for a larger one, compare the result of a query with a WHERE, or whole tables with
**Tools ▸ Compare…**. Comparing only reads.

## Export the report

**Export Report…** saves what the compare found as **HTML** (to read or send), **CSV** (every difference on its own
line, for a spreadsheet) or **Markdown** (for a ticket). HTML and Markdown list up to 1,000 rows per table.

## Limits

- More than 100,000 differing rows in one table are reported as too many to list, without sync statements for that
  table: narrow the compare with a WHERE, or copy the table instead.
- Column order and row formats are compared and synced. Partitioning is only noticed on one side: a table partitioned
  differently on both reads the same, and no statement adds or removes it. System versioning isn't compared.
- The data compare reads each side as it goes, not one snapshot: on a busy table it can show rows that changed meanwhile.
- A FLOAT compares by the text the server gives, about six digits: 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 both read `1`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html

# AI agents

Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop and other MCP clients can use AirSQL to read your schemas, run read-only
queries, profile tables and propose SQL for you to run. They work through AirSQL on your Mac, so they see only what you
allow, never your passwords, and can't change data.

## Turn agents on

1. Choose **AirSQL ▸ Settings…** (⌘,), then **Agents**, and tick **Allow AI agents to use AirSQL**.
2. Under **Connections**, choose what agents may do with each connection. Every connection starts at **Off**.
3. Add AirSQL to your agent:
   - **Add to Claude Code…** or **Add to Gemini CLI…**: AirSQL shows the exact change to that program's settings
     (`~/.claude.json` or `~/.gemini/settings.json`), and makes it only when you click **Add**, keeping the old file as
     `.airsql-backup`. Restart the program afterwards.
   - Claude Code's plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add kleash/airsql`, then `claude plugin install airsql@airsql`.
   - Claude Desktop: open `airsql.mcpb` from AirSQL's release.
   - Another client: **Copy** gives the command, `/Applications/AirSQL.app/Contents/MacOS/AirSQL --mcp`.

The connection must be connected in AirSQL for an agent to read it.

## Access levels

| Level | Agents may |
|---|---|
| Off | not see the connection at all |
| Schema | read databases, tables, columns, keys and indexes, and find columns by name; put SQL into a query tab |
| Schema + read | also run read-only queries and see query plans, within the row cap and time limit of Settings ▸ Safety |
| Schema + read + analytics | also profile tables, get ten times the rows and four times the time, and save results to files |

**Sample rows** (a separate switch) lets agents see a few rows of each table they describe. Only you can change these:
no agent can, whatever it asks.

## What keeps your data safe

- An agent's statement runs only if AirSQL can prove it reads and nothing more: one SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE or
  EXPLAIN, without locking clauses, `INTO`, hints or functions such as `SLEEP` ([what passes](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html)).
- It then runs on a session of its own that the server keeps read-only, inside a read-only transaction that is rolled
  back, with a time limit. Even a statement that slipped past the check can't write.
- To change something, an agent puts the SQL into a query tab. Nothing runs until you press Run.
- For more safety still, connect with a database user that can only read.

## Agents in AirSQL's windows

Agents can also work in AirSQL's windows as you do: open tabs, choose menu commands, fill in sheets, take screenshots.
Whatever that would change waits for you:

- Anything that would run on a server (Run in a query tab, Apply, a compare's sync, Restore, Copy, CSV import, Commit)
  first shows the SQL preview sheet, marked **Asked by** and the agent's name. Only you can press its Run; the agent
  can only decline. Statements that AirSQL proves only read run without asking.
- Agents can't change Settings, agent access, a connection's colour, read-only switch, server, route, login, TLS,
  startup SQL or safety settings, nor save files, start an export, save a password, trust a certificate, paste from
  your clipboard, quit AirSQL or press a button marked destructive (Don't Save, Disconnect with a transaction open).
  Text an agent types into a query tab of a Production connection is shown to you first.
- On connections whose agent access doesn't include reading, grids and results, the filters their values go into,
  the tab's messages (a server's error can quote a value) and the SQL preview's statements are hidden from the
  agent's snapshots and screenshots; the SQL log's text always is. A cell's right-click menu never shows an agent the
  cell's value or your clipboard's text.

**Settings ▸ Safety ▸ Ask before agents change anything** (on by default, per connection in its Safety tab) turns the
asking off; what is yours alone stays yours.

## See what agents did

The agents' item in the status bar says what they're doing. Click it (or choose **Tools ▸ Agents ▸ Agent Activity**)
for every call since AirSQL opened, with how it ended. A call that reads a database also shows in Activity, where
**Cancel** stops it. **Turn Agents Off** in that popover (or in Tools ▸ Agents) stops them at once.

**View ▸ Agent Results** opens the connection's Agent tab: every statement agents ran on it with `run_queries`, newest
last, and under the list the rows the selected one got, read-only and no more than the agent got. Double-click a
`run_queries` call in Agent Activity to open the tab at its statements. Double-click a statement (or choose **Query ▸
Open in New Query**) to put it in a new query tab, where you can change it and run it yourself. The tab keeps the
last 100 statements since AirSQL opened.

## Files agents save

With analytics, agents can save query results as CSV or JSON files. They go only to the **Agent Exports** folder in
AirSQL's settings folder (Settings ▸ Agents ▸ Exports ▸ Show in Finder), readable by you alone.

## The fine print

Agents reach AirSQL through a socket in AirSQL's settings folder that only you can open, with a key that changes each
time AirSQL starts. Other programs running as you could read that key too, as with any app of yours.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/liquibase.html

# Liquibase changelogs

AirSQL writes [Liquibase](https://www.liquibase.com) changelogs in Liquibase's **formatted SQL**: plain SQL with
`--changeset author:id` lines, which Liquibase reads as it is. You can write one of a whole database, save a compare's
sync script as changesets, or save any change AirSQL shows you before it runs. AirSQL only writes the files: run them
with your own `liquibase` (`liquibase update`, `liquibase rollback-count 1`…).

## A changelog of a database

**Tools ▸ Generate Liquibase Changelog…** writes a changelog of a database of the connection the window is about.

- **Content**: **Structure** writes the objects' DDL, **Rows** their rows as DML, **Both** the two.
- The list holds the database's tables, views, procedures, functions, triggers, events and sequences, each ticked.
  Untick what you don't want; space ticks the selected rows, double-click ticks one, and the right-click menu
  includes all, none or the selected rows; the filter above the list narrows it, and all and none then mean the
  objects shown. For **DML**, tick **Rows** for the tables whose rows to write, and type a
  **WHERE** condition (double-click the cell) to write only some of them, such as `active = 1`.
- **Author** and **Ids** make each `--changeset` line (see [Settings](#settings) below). **Rollback** adds the
  `--rollback` line that undoes each object. **Skip what already exists** adds preconditions that mark a changeset
  as ran, rather than run it, when its object is already in the database: handy for a database made before you used
  Liquibase.
- **Files**: one file, or a folder with a file per changeset and `db.changelog-master.yaml`, which includes them in
  order: point Liquibase at that one.

The preview beside the form shows the changelog as it will be written. **Save Changelog** reads each table's rows
then, in key order, from one consistent snapshot; the work is listed in the activity list, with **Stop**. Nothing is
left behind if it fails or you stop it.

### What the changelog holds, in order

Each object gets one changeset, in an order that runs cleanly on an empty database:

1. sequences, then tables, each without its foreign keys and without its next AUTO_INCREMENT value;
2. the tables' rows (parents before children), as INSERTs of 100 rows each;
3. the foreign keys, one changeset each (`ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT`);
4. functions and procedures, then views (each after the views it reads), triggers and events.

Rows come before foreign keys and triggers, so neither gets in their way. A changeset of rows first sets the session
as the rows were read: in UTC (TIMESTAMP values stay as they were), without strict mode (zero dates load) and with
`NO_AUTO_VALUE_ON_ZERO` (a 0 in an AUTO_INCREMENT column stays 0); it puts the session's own settings back at its end.
A table with zero dates or TIMESTAMP defaults gets the same around its `CREATE TABLE`.

Attributes are added only where they are needed:

- A procedure, function, trigger or event holds semicolons of its own, so its changeset says `splitStatements:false`
  and runs it as one statement (or ends it with `//` and says `endDelimiter://`, as you choose in Settings).
- `stripComments:false` keeps comments Liquibase would otherwise remove, such as MySQL's `/*!80023 INVISIBLE */`.
- Views are written as `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` with `runOnChange:true`: edit a view in the changelog and Liquibase
  replaces it.
- A comment line in a routine that Liquibase would read as one of its own (`-- rollback …`, `-- changeset …`)
  becomes a `#` comment, which MySQL and MariaDB read the same way.

Every changeset AirSQL writes is read back the way Liquibase reads it before it is saved; if Liquibase would split it
differently from how it runs here, AirSQL says so and doesn't write it.

## Save a change as a changeset

When the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html) shows a change (the table editor, a view or routine, a sync script), tick
**Save as Liquibase changeset**: once the change has run, a sheet shows the changeset. In the query tab, select the
statements (or put the insertion point in one) and choose **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…**. In the compare window,
**Save as Changeset…** (or **Query ▸ Save as Changeset…** in its “Sync script” tab) saves the sync script: a changeset
per structure step and one per run of row changes on a table, destructive steps saying so in their `--comment`.

Choose the changelog to add to (**Choose…**), or start one (**New…**). The changesets go at its end and their ids carry
on its numbering. A change keeps only what Liquibase runs: `USE` and the transaction around it are left out (each
changeset runs in a transaction of its own), and so is the database the change named its objects with, so the
changeset runs in whichever database Liquibase updates. A change made on a session with `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` in its
sql_mode turns that on for its statements and back off after, so a backslash in its strings stays a backslash. A
`--rollback` is added when every statement of the change can be undone: DROP for what it creates, DROP COLUMN for an
added column, DROP INDEX and DROP FOREIGN KEY for added keys, RENAME back. Row changes and drops get none.

## Settings

**Settings ▸ Liquibase** holds:

- **Author**: who the changesets are by; empty uses your Mac account's name.
- **Ids**: `{date}` (20261102), `{time}` (141500), `{n}` (001, 002…, counting on from the changesets a changelog has)
  and `{object}` (the table, view or routine). An id that is already taken gets `-2`, `-3`….
- **Changelog files**: one file, or a folder with a file per changeset.
- **Routines**: as the changeset's only statement (`splitStatements:false`), or with each statement ended by `//`
  (`endDelimiter://`). A change with several statements and a routine among them always uses `//`.
- **Leave DEFINER out** of views, routines, triggers and events (on at first), so they run as whoever runs the
  changelog rather than as an account the other server may not have.
- **Add --rollback** where it can be written (on at first).

## Limits

- Routines keep the sql_mode of the session Liquibase runs them in, not the one they were made with.
- Liquibase reads `${name}` in a changeset as a property it may replace; text like that in your data or routines is
  replaced when you define such a property.
- Generated columns are left out of the INSERTs: their values follow from the others.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/accessibility.html

# Accessibility

AirSQL is built from the Mac's own controls wherever it can be, and labels the ones it draws itself for VoiceOver.

## VoiceOver

- The data grid reads as a table: its column names and types, cell values, sort order and row counts, and which rows
  are changed, added or marked for deletion.
- A connection says its state and its marks (Production, read-only) in words, not only by its colour.
- AirSQL announces what happens away from the focus: a statement's error or note, a Test Connection result, and the end
  of a Find Text search.
- In the ER diagram each table reads with its columns; pressing it opens its structure.

## Keyboard

Every command is in the menu bar, and **Help ▸ Keyboard Shortcuts** lists them all. ⌥⌘1, ⌥⌘2 and ⌥⌘3 go to the sidebar,
the editor and the results; ⌃⇥ moves between tabs. To show, hide and find columns in a grid without the mouse, use
**View ▸ Column List**.

## Motion and text size

Sidebar and tree animations stop under **Reduce Motion**. ⌘+ and ⌘− change the text size of the SQL editor and the grid
in focus; the rest of the window stays at its size.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/shortcuts.html

# Keyboard shortcuts

Every command is in the menu bar, with its shortcut next to it, and right-click menus show the same commands. Hold
the pointer over a menu item to see what it does. A greyed-out item says why it is off. **Help ▸ Keyboard Shortcuts**
lists them all in the app, narrowed as you type.

⇥ Tab moves from field to field and list to list, from the sidebar on into the tab that shows. In the SQL editor, where
Tab indents, ⌥⌘1 goes to the sidebar and ⌥⌘3 to the results. ⌃⇥ and ⌃⇧⇥ show the next and previous tab, as in Safari.

F2 renames what has the focus, as in HeidiSQL: the table, view or folder selected in the sidebar (on a connection, it
opens Edit…), else the tab shown
(a query tab that isn't saved in a file). In a grid, F2 edits the focused cell, as Return does; a cell that can't be
edited (a query result's) shows its value in the value panel.

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/privacy-security.html

# Privacy and security

AirSQL holds the keys to your databases, so it is careful by default: it talks only to the servers you set up, your
passwords stay in your Keychain, and nothing changes on a server until you say so.

## What AirSQL connects to

Only the database servers, SSH hosts and proxies you add. It has no account, no ads and no analytics, and it doesn't
check for updates by itself (Homebrew does: `brew upgrade --cask airsql`). The Help menu opens pages in your browser.

## Your passwords

- They are kept in your Keychain, never in AirSQL's settings file, in its logs, in the [SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html) or in
  what AI agents see.
- A PAM or LDAP login sends the password as plain text, so AirSQL uses one only when you turn it on for the connection,
  and only over TLS that proves the server is the right one.

## Your connections

- TLS is checked against the server's real name, also through an SSH tunnel. A certificate macOS doesn't know is shown
  with its fingerprint for you to [trust](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html), and AirSQL warns you if it ever changes.
- Tunnels and proxies end in a private socket on your Mac, never in a network port that other apps or computers could
  use.
- A server can't make AirSQL read files on your Mac (`LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` is off), and AirSQL sends one statement
  at a time.
- A lost connection is reported, never quietly reconnected: that would lose an open transaction without a word.

## Your data

- Nothing is written until you choose Run or Apply. Changes show their SQL first
  ([Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html)), and Apply checks that each change touched exactly the rows it should.
- A connection coloured **Production** starts with stricter safety checks ([Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html#safety)).
- A **read-only** connection runs only what AirSQL can prove reads, on sessions the server keeps read-only
  ([Connections](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html#add-or-edit-a-connection)).

## AI agents

Agents can't use AirSQL until you allow them. Then each connection has its own access level, an agent's queries must
pass the [read-only check](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html), and a change it asks for waits for your approval. Agents never see
saved passwords.

## The app itself

AirSQL is signed by its developer, uses macOS's hardened runtime and is notarized by Apple. Its one library, MariaDB
Connector/C with OpenSSL, is built from pinned, checked sources, and every release includes that source and a list of
what is inside (an SBOM). Every change is scanned for known vulnerabilities, leaked secrets and security bugs. More in
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/kleash/airsql/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Check a download

Every release lists the zip's SHA-256. In Terminal, in the folder where the download is:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c AirSQL-X.Y.Z.zip.sha256
```

Once AirSQL is in Applications, `spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/AirSQL.app` says
`source=Notarized Developer ID`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting

AirSQL says what went wrong in plain words, followed by the server's own error with its number. Here is what to do
about the common problems.

## A connection fails

The message offers **Try Again**, **Edit Connection…** and this page.

| AirSQL says | What to do |
|---|---|
| Can't find the server | Check the host name, and that you are on the right network or VPN. |
| The server refused the connection | Check the port, and that the database server is running. |
| The server didn't answer in time | Check the host name and the port: a firewall may be dropping the connection. |
| The server can't be reached from this network | Turn on the VPN, or connect through an SSH host that can reach the server. |
| The server didn't accept the user name or password | Check both. Through an SSH host, the server sees the SSH host's address, and the account must allow that host. |
| This user may not log in from this computer's address | An administrator can allow it (the account's host part). |
| The server only accepts encrypted connections | Turn on TLS for the connection. |
| The server doesn't offer TLS | Choose **Edit Connection…**, then in the TLS tab set TLS to **Off**, only for a server on this Mac or a network you trust end to end. |
| The server asked for a login method AirSQL doesn't allow on this connection | A PAM or LDAP account: turn on its plain-text login for the connection, with TLS that proves the server. |
| The server blocked this computer after too many failed connections | An administrator can unblock it (`FLUSH HOSTS`). |

## AirSQL asks about the server's certificate

See [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html). If AirSQL warns that a certificate has changed and nobody told you it would,
choose **Cancel** and ask the server's administrator.

## "The connection to the server was lost"

AirSQL doesn't reconnect by itself, because a quiet reconnect would lose an open transaction without telling you.
Reconnect when you are ready. Changes you hadn't committed were rolled back by the server.

## macOS asks about the local network

To reach a server on your local network, choose **Allow** when macOS asks whether AirSQL may find and connect to
devices on it. If you chose **Don't Allow**: System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Local Network, then turn on AirSQL.

## AirSQL doesn't open

It needs macOS 13.1 or later. Downloads from the releases page and Homebrew are notarized and open normally.

## No help pages show

The help is on the web. On a Mac that can't reach it, **Help ▸ AirSQL Help Offline** opens the same text, kept in the app.

## Report a problem

**Help ▸ Report a Problem** opens a form on GitHub with your AirSQL and macOS versions filled in. **Help ▸ Copy
Diagnostics** copies those versions and the client library's (no names, hosts or paths). **AirSQL ▸ About AirSQL**
shows AirSQL's version and the client library's, with links to this site and to the licences of AirSQL and the
libraries in it. The [SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html) shows exactly what AirSQL sent: read it before you share any of it, because
it holds your queries.


---

Source: https://github.com/kleash/airsql/blob/main/Resources/AgentGuide.md

# AirSQL agent guide

AirSQL is a Mac app for MySQL and MariaDB. Through its MCP server you can read the schemas of the connections the
person at the Mac allows, run read-only queries, profile tables, propose SQL in a console tab for the person to edit
and run, and drive AirSQL's windows as they do. You never see passwords, and you can't change data, connections or
settings on your own: whatever would change something waits for the person at the Mac (see gate), and each
connection's access level is their choice alone.

## overview

1. `context` first: the connections you may use (name, id, access level, MySQL or MariaDB and its version, current
   database, schema hash, row cap and timeout), the person's active connection and the open console tabs. A connection
   whose access is Off isn't listed; `hiddenConnections` counts them.
2. `get_schema` once per connection: every database's tables in one compact reply. Keep its `hash` and pass it back as
   `if_changed_from` later: an unchanged schema answers `{unchanged: true}` and costs nothing.
3. `describe` the tables you'll query (columns, keys both ways, indexes, CREATE statement, row estimates).
   `search_columns` finds a column by name (`email`, `*_id`) in every database without reading the whole schema.
4. `run_queries` with several statements at once; `explain` a slow one; `profile` a table you don't know yet.
5. To change anything, write the SQL and call `open_in_console`: the person reads it, edits it, runs it. Then
   `read_console` shows what they ran and the result or error.
6. To work in AirSQL's windows (open a table, use a menu, fill a sheet), `snapshot` first, then `menu`, `press`, `set`,
   `type`, `key` and the clicks, and `wait` for what they start (see ui and screens).

Connections must be connected in AirSQL (by the person) before the database tools work on them. After a relaunch, tabs
other than consoles are placeholders: they hold names only, and they connect nothing until their button is pressed.

## access

Each connection has one level, set by the person in Settings ▸ Agents (or the connection's Agents tab):

- **Off** (the default; Production connections start here): invisible to agents.
- **Schema**: `get_schema`, `describe`, `search_columns`, the schema resource, `open_in_console`; `read_console` without
  result rows.
- **Schema + read**: also `run_queries` and `explain`, within the connection's row cap and timeout (Settings ▸ Safety:
  10,000 rows and 30 s by default, 1,000 and 15 s on Production).
- **Schema + read + analytics**: also `profile`, `to_file`, ten times the rows and four times the timeout.

Sample rows are a separate switch: when on, `describe` shows a few rows of each table. A call beyond the level is refused
with the level it needs. Ask the person to change a level; you can't.

## read-only

Statements you write run only when AirSQL's classifier proves them read-only: one statement, `SELECT`,
`WITH … SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE` or `EXPLAIN` (not `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). It refuses `INTO`, `FOR UPDATE`,
`LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, optimizer hints, temporary tables, and functions such as `SLEEP`, `BENCHMARK`, `GET_LOCK`,
`LOAD_FILE` and stored functions. Each statement then runs on AirSQL's own agent session, which is read-only, inside
`START TRANSACTION READ ONLY` … `ROLLBACK`, with the server's statement timeout and a watchdog. Both guards always apply.
A refused statement comes back with `ok: false` and the reason; the other statements of the call still run.
The person sees each statement you ran and the rows you got in the connection's Agent tab (View ▸ Agent Results).

## tools

- `context {}`: start here.
- `get_schema {connection, databases?, format?: compact | ddl, if_changed_from?}`: compact lines look like
  `orders: id bigint PK AI, customer_id int NULL → customers.id, total decimal(12,2) ='0.00'; KEY(customer_id)`:
  PK primary key, AI auto-increment, NULL nullable, `=` default, `→` foreign key, then composite keys and indexes, and
  `-- comment`. Views start with `view`, sequences with `sequence`. System databases are left out unless named. A
  database too big for the reply comes as names only: name it, or describe its tables.
- `describe {connection, objects: ["table" or "db.table"], database?}`: names in backquotes may contain dots.
- `search_columns {connection, pattern, type?, databases?}`: from AirSQL's schema cache, so no query runs. `pattern` is
  part of a column's name, or a whole name with `*` and `?`; `type` a data type (`varchar`, `json`, `*text`); neither
  minds case. Each match has `database`, `table`, `column`, `type` (as `varchar(255)`), `nullable`, and `primaryKey`
  and `kind` (`view`, `sequence`) when they apply. At most 500 (`capped: true` means more matched). Databases whose
  columns aren't loaded yet (a very big server) are searched once you name them.
- `run_queries {connection, database?, queries: [{sql, max_rows?}], format?: json | csv, to_file?}`: 200 rows per
  statement unless `max_rows` says more (up to the row cap); `capped: true` means there were more. `types` names each
  column's type as AirSQL's grid does (`bigint unsigned`, `varchar`, `datetime`). Values are text (binary as 0x…
  hex), NULL is null in JSON and an empty field in CSV, long values are cut at 2,000 characters.
  `to_file: true` (analytics) writes each result to a CSV or JSON file in AirSQL's agent export folder and answers with
  its path, rows and size instead of the rows.
- `profile {connection, table, database?, columns?, where?}`: row count, and per column NULLs, distinct values, min,
  max, average (numbers) and the five most common values, computed on the server.
- `explain {connection, sql, database?, format?: traditional | json}`.
- `open_in_console {sql, title?, connection?}`: never runs anything.
- `read_console {tab?}`: by id or title from `context`; default the active console tab.
- `guide {topic?}`: this guide.

Long calls send progress notifications when your client asks for them (`_meta.progressToken`).

## resources

Each connected connection you may read has its compact schema as a resource, `airsql://<connection name>/schema`
(percent-encoded), the same text as `get_schema`. `resources/list` lists them.

## recipes

- **Answer a question about the data**: `context` → `get_schema` → `describe` the tables involved → `run_queries`
  with a `COUNT(*)` first, then the query, with `max_rows` small.
- **Analyse a big result**: with analytics, `run_queries` with `to_file: true`, then read the file with your own tools.
- **Change data or structure**: write the statements, then `open_in_console` with a clear title; tell the person what
  they do. After they run them, `read_console`.
- **Find where something is kept**: `search_columns` with part of its name (`email`, `*_at` with type `datetime`),
  then `describe` the tables it found.
- **Check a query's cost**: `explain` it, look for full scans (`type: ALL`) on big tables, `describe` for indexes.

## ui

The UI tools act in AirSQL's windows as the person would; replies are JSON as text (`screenshot`: a PNG), `isError` on
failure, and every reply after an action carries the sheet it opened, if any.

- `snapshot {include?, in?}`: windows, sidebar, tabs, status bar, activity and open sheets by default; `menus` lists
  every menu-bar command with its shortcut and, when off, why; `elements` the accessibility tree (id, role, title,
  value, frame in points from the window's top left); `settings` the saved settings.
- `screenshot {target?: main | sheet | window:<title> | element:<id>, scale?: 1 | 2}`: drawn by AirSQL itself.
- `menu {path}`: "Query > Run Statement"; after a right-click, "context > Copy".
- `press {id | title, in?}`: buttons, checkboxes, segments, links. A pop-up is chosen with `set`.
- `set {id | title, value, in?}`: text fields, checkboxes (true or false), pop-ups and segments (the option's title),
  and the console's editor (`console.editor`: the whole text).
- `select {pane: sidebar | tabs, names}` selects connections or a tab by name; without pane, rows of a list in the
  frontmost sheet or window.
- `type {text}` types where the cursor is; `key {combo}` presses keys as the keyboard does ("cmd+return", "escape").
- `click {x, y, count?, button?, modifiers?, in?}`, `double_click {x, y}` (opens or edits), `right_click {x, y}`
  (answers with the menu it opens). Points come from `snapshot` frames or a scale-1 screenshot.
- `wait {until: sheet | no_sheet | popover | idle | text, text?, timeout?}`: idle means nothing runs.

Open and Save panels can't be driven: press Cancel, or leave them to the person.

## gate

AirSQL's agents' gate fails closed. While it carries out your request, nothing that could change something runs on
its own:

- **The SQL preview sheet is the person's.** Run in a console, Apply in the grid and the editors, a compare's sync,
  Restore, Copy and CSV import show what will run in the SQL preview sheet, marked "Asked by <your client>". Only the
  person can press its Run (or Return, or click it): you get "Only the person at the Mac can approve…". You may press
  Decline (`preview.cancel`), and `wait {until: no_sheet}` for their answer. A console run of statements that are all
  proven read-only (see read-only) runs without asking.
- **Statements on the person's sessions** that what you did sends, and that aren't proven read-only (a Commit, a
  Roll Back, the transaction mode, a Kill), wait in the same sheet, one by one.
- **A read-only connection** refuses in the console (and the navigator, a sync, Restore and CSV import) any statement
  that isn't proven read-only, a bare USE aside, before anything asks: there is nothing to approve. A table tab's WHERE
  filter must pass the same check inside its SELECT. Open in Terminal starts a read-only session there; the process
  list's Kill (the person's sheet) still works, as it changes no data.
- **The person's alone, even with approval:** agent access levels and sample rows, a connection's colour (production),
  read-only switch, server, route, login and safety settings, every Safety setting (this gate's switch among them),
  whether agents are allowed, the client tools AirSQL runs, and every other setting but the look (theme, font sizes,
  rows per page, the NULL text). Other saved data (names, folders, the look) is refused too while Settings ▸ Safety ▸
  Ask before agents change anything is on. The Settings window is to look at.
- **Files, the clipboard, trust:** you can't save a console's file, start an export, save a Liquibase changelog, save
  or remember a password, trust a certificate or SSH host key, or paste (the clipboard is the person's); use `type` or
  `set` for text, and run_queries `to_file` for results. A button marked destructive (Don't Save, Disconnect with a
  transaction open, Delete, Clear) is the person's call, and so is Quit. The connection editor opens for you, but its
  Save keeps nothing that is the person's.
- **A production console's text:** `type` or `set` into the editor of a console on a connection coloured Production
  shows the person the text first; single keys that would change it are refused.
- **Data you may not read is hidden:** on connections below Schema + read, grids, query results (and the value panel,
  View As, charts, Column Summary and the status bar's figure), the filters a value goes into (`result.filter`,
  `tableData.where`, `values.list`, `quickFilter.value`), the process list, a compare's rows and sync script, the
  console's Messages (`console.messages`: a server's error can quote a value), an EXPLAIN's tree (`console.planTree`)
  and the SQL preview's statements (`preview.sql`) are covered in screenshots ("Hidden from agents") and left out of
  snapshots (`hidden`: no value, title or help; `set` still types into a hidden field). The SQL log's text
  (`sqlLog.text`: every connection's statements) is hidden from you on every connection. A cell's right-click Quick
  Filter ▸ lists the Data menu's items for you (Equal to Selection…), never the value or the clipboard's text.

The person can turn the asking off for a connection or for all (Settings ▸ Safety); person-only things stay theirs.

## screens

Ids for `press`, `set` and `screenshot element:<id>`; `snapshot include elements` lists what is on screen now.

- **Main window toolbar**: `toolbar.connection`, `toolbar.database`, `toolbar.run`, `toolbar.runAll`,
  `toolbar.explain`, `toolbar.transactionMode`, `toolbar.commit`, `toolbar.rollback`, `toolbar.cancel`.
- **Sidebar**: `sidebar.filter`, `sidebar.connections` (select with `select pane=sidebar`), `sidebar.newConnection`,
  `sidebar.processes`. With nothing open: `firstRun.addConnection`, `firstRun.setUpAgents`; a connection's summary:
  `summary.connect` (`summary.disconnect` once it is connecting or connected), `summary.newQuery`, `summary.edit`.
- **Tabs**: `tabs`, `tabs.new`, each `tab` with `tab.close` (select with `select pane=tabs`), `tab.rename`.
- **Navigator** (a connection's tree in the sidebar; double-click opens): a database `database.tables`; text views
  `navigator.text`; Find Text `find.text`, `find.scope`, `find.go`, `find.stop`, `find.results`, `find.status`;
  processes `processes.list`, `processes.refresh`, `processes.interval`, `processes.killQuery`,
  `processes.killConnection`; sheets `newDatabase.name`, `rename.name`, `copyTable.name`, `copyTable.database`,
  `copyTable.where`, `copyTable.rows`, `bulk.database`, `bulk.engine`.
- **Connection editor** (File ▸ New Connection, Connection ▸ Edit…; Save is the person's for what is theirs):
  `editor.tabs`, `editor.name`, `editor.folder`, `editor.comment`, `editor.database`, `editor.databaseFilter`, and
  the person's `editor.colour`, `editor.host`, `editor.port`, `editor.socket`, `editor.user`, `editor.password`,

- **Grid** (results, table data): `grid`, `grid.header`, `grid.rowNumbers`, `grid.editor` (Return or F2 opens it on the

  `grid.position`, `grid.figure`; the value panel `valuePanel` (`valuePanel.mode`, `valuePanel.text`, `valuePanel.tree`,

  `grid.chart` (`chart.kind`, `chart.x`, `chart.y`); Column List `columnList.search`, `columnList.table`; Column
  Summary `columnSummary` (a `columnSummary.value` filters by it); Go to Row `goToRow.text`. A console result filters
  its own rows (Data ▸ Quick Filter, Filter by Values…, Sort by Columns…, Search All Columns): its bar

- **Table tab** (a table's rows: Database ▸ Open Data or a double-click in the tree; a single click shows them in the
  preview tab): `tableData`; its grid bar `tableData.scope` (where filtering runs), `tableData.where` (a WHERE condition:
  set it, then key `return` applies it), `tableData.recentFilters`, `tableData.clearFilter`, `tableData.search`, `tableData.loadedOnly`,
  `tableData.busy`; the notice `tableData.notice` (`tableData.noticeText`, `tableData.preview`, `tableData.revert`,
  `tableData.apply`: Apply opens the SQL preview, whose Run is the person's); the status bar's `tableData.count`,
  `tableData.loadMore`, `tableData.loadAll`; find bar (⌘F) `find.text`, `find.replaceText`, `find.options`,
  `find.previous`, `find.next`, `find.count`, `find.replace`, `find.replaceAll`, `find.done`; Export Rows `export.rows`,
  `export.format`, `export.headers`, `export.null`, `export.crlf`, `export.copy`, `export.save` (the person's),
  `export.cancel`; Filter by Values `values.search`, `values.list`, `values.all`, `values.none`, `values.ok`,
  `values.cancel`; Data ▸ Quick Filter ▸ Type a Value… `quickFilter.operator`, `quickFilter.value`, `quickFilter.add`
  (then press Filter); Data ▸ Sort by Columns… `sort.column.N`, `sort.direction.N`, `sort.up.N`, `sort.down.N`,
  `sort.remove.N` (N from 0, the first sort column first), `sort.add`, `sort.ok`, `sort.cancel`. Edits wait as pending changes until Apply. Typing a value checks it by the column's type first. Return
  or a double-click on an ENUM cell shows its values as a menu; on a SET cell a checklist `grid.set` (`grid.set.member`
  checkboxes, `grid.set.done`, `grid.set.cancel`); on a foreign key cell the referenced rows `grid.lookup`
  (`grid.lookup.search`, `grid.lookup.rows`; Return picks); a one-column foreign key's cell shows the referenced row's
  label after its value. A column header's menu (and the Data menu) has Use as Label, Add Virtual Foreign Key… (a sheet
  with `virtualKey.table`; kept on this Mac, never in the database) and Remove Virtual Foreign Key. Data ▸ Insert Value ▸ puts in NOW(), UUID() and the like;
  Paste, Paste as New Rows and Paste with Format… (its sheet `pasteFormat.separator`, `pasteFormat.decimal`,
  `pasteFormat.dateOrder`) are the person's (the clipboard is). Query ▸ Edit as Table opens the selected INSERT
  statements in their table's tab as new rows; Apply then shows the SQL preview. Quit is the person's too: it lists pending changes
  and open transactions first.
- **Console result editing**: a console result of a one-table SELECT that includes the key, or of an inner join with
  every table's key, edits like a table tab (`grid.editor`, the pick-lists and foreign key drop-down, Data ▸ Set NULL, Set DEFAULT, Insert
  Value, Delete Rows in a one-table result, Undo, Revert); the status bar's `result.editState` says Editable or Read-only (its tooltip says why), and a double-click on
  a read-only cell says why in `grid.readOnlyReason`. Pending changes show in the notice `tableData.notice`
  (`tableData.apply`, `tableData.preview`, `tableData.revert`); Apply opens the SQL preview, whose Run is the person's.

## troubleshooting

- "isn't running, or agents are off": open AirSQL and turn on Settings ▸ Agents ▸ Allow AI agents to use AirSQL.
- "No connection … is open to agents": use a name or id from `context`; the person may have set it to Off.
- "isn't connected": ask the person to connect it in AirSQL.
- "needs Schema + read" (or analytics): the person can raise the level in Settings ▸ Agents.
- "Refused": the statement isn't provably read-only; rewrite it as one plain SELECT, or propose it with
  `open_in_console`.
- "Stopped at the agent timeout": narrow the query (WHERE, LIMIT), or ask for the analytics level.
- "Only the person at the Mac can approve…" or "…can change…": that is the gate; tell the person what waits for them.
- "The person at the Mac declined": nothing ran; ask what they want instead.
- "Settings are the person's", "The clipboard is the person's": use `snapshot include settings` to read settings, and
  `type` or `set` instead of pasting.
